- **Sticks for `--press`**: the pseudo-buttons ls-up, ls-down, ls-left, ls-right and rs-up ... rs-right push one stick
  axis all the way while they are held (`pad_script`). A scripted run now walks Michael through the bank, brings up the
  phone (up), calls (Cross), sets off the charge, and reaches the alarm-lit vault corridor (run 080).
- **SPU coverage by runs, as designed** (D-076, D-099): each run's misses and the images it saves (`--spu-dump`) go into
  the next `scripts/lift-spu.sh`. Five rounds took the session from 586 million interpreted SPU instructions (and 4.3
  billion in the round where the charge brought 27 new images) to none.
- **Tried and dropped**: treating `ila` offsets in position-independent SPU code as function entries (the offset of a
  callback, then an add of where the job was loaded). It found real callbacks, but some candidates were data. Lifted as
  code, they marked data words as lifted instructions; a job's DMA into its own buffers then counted as overwriting
  lifted code (D-085), dropped the job's program, and the binary was interpreted for the rest of the run: 54.6 billion
  instructions, 10 fps. Entry points come only from the code's own branches and calls, absolute constants, and what
  runs actually entered. The lift was redone from every log, without them.
- **NV4097_SET_BEGIN_END with an invalid primitive** (GTA V sends 36 now and then in the mission): a warning, and the
  draw keeps the primitive it had, as RPCS3 (`set_begin_end`); not a failure. It drew points before.
- Test: the D-104 yield test checks the thread's backoff state instead of a 2 ms bound, which a loaded machine
  overran.

## D-109 · 2026-10-05 · SPU images and shader programs found again without hashing them again

A profile of the first mission at 30 fps (run 081, `sample`, 10 s) showed 1.3 cores busy: the SPU workers about 95%
of a core, the RSX thread 18%, the game's PPU threads under 10%.
- **SPU images**: every job and module load hashed the whole image (`ps_spu_hash64`, one lane) and searched the
  registry linearly under its lock: 363 samples. Each worker now keeps the images it identified (256, direct-mapped by
  guest address, size and LS address) with a four-lane content hash, four times as fast; the same bytes at the same
  place are the same program. Only lifted programs are kept, and only while the registry is unchanged
  (`ps_spu_registry_generation`, bumped by every register and unregister). 30 samples.
- **Shader programs**: the compile a fragment program maps to, per set of translation options, is kept with the
  decoded program (and the vertex program's with it), instead of building its words and a string key every draw. A
  fragment program set again is decoded again only when its bytes changed, checked by its watch (it was decoded on
  every set). GTA V copies its fragment programs with their constants patched for most draws, so most still change;
  what is left is under 1% of a core.
- **Texture checks** are counted in the per-frame report: 560 to 780 a frame in the mission, 33 to 40 MB hashed, about
  1 ms of the RSX thread. Write protection would make them free, but host code that writes guest memory through the
  kernel (`read()` into a guest buffer) would get EFAULT instead of a fault the tracker can handle: not done.
- Tests: an image loaded again is the program found before unless its bytes or the registry changed; draws reuse a
  program's compile until the CPU rewrites it; a program the RSX rewrites between two draws of one batch and sets again
  is decoded again.

## D-110 · 2026-10-05 · Render targets reload from guest memory in every format, and keep what was rendered

When the RSX itself, or (through `invalidate_memory`) anything the runtime sees, writes guest memory under a render
target, the target reloads from it before the GPU uses it again. Three gaps, none hit by GTA V's first mission, all
generic:
- **Formats**: the reload only took A8R8G8B8 colour targets (a texture decode and a draw); every other format was
  refused, and depth buffers were never reloaded. Now every format the readback writes (A8B8G8R8 and its X forms,
  W16Z16Y16X16 and W32Z32Y32X32 float, X32 float, B8, Z16, Z24S8) reloads by the inverse of `store_readback`: its bytes
  in the Metal format, a staging buffer and a blit (Z24S8's depth and stencil apart). Depth buffers reload when a pass
  opens over them.
- **An open pass**: a target of the pass already open was never reloaded, because the pass went on (`open_pass` and
  `do_clear` kept it). It now ends, and the next one reloads.
- **What the GPU rendered**: an RSX write into part of a target (NV308A, the NV3089 destination, an NV0039
  destination) reloaded the target from guest memory that never had the GPU's rendering, so it was lost. The targets
  under the write go to guest memory first (`flush_memory`), so the reload has both. A deferred NV0039 copy reads back
  its destination's targets with its source's, at the point in the GPU's order where the copy is.
- Run: the first mission as before, 30 fps, one failure (MSAA), no new readbacks.
- Tests: every format round-trips through a CPU write and a reload, but the pixel a 1x1 clear covers; an NV308A pixel
  written over a rendered target keeps the triangle and the clear; the NV0039 front end flushes its destination.

## D-111 · 2026-10-05 · Swizzled colour targets write back and reload in Morton order

A swizzled render target (NV4097_SET_SURFACE_FORMAT type 2) keeps its texels in Morton order (`morton_index`, as
swizzled textures). Its write-back and reload (D-110) refused it. Now a colour target of power-of-two size, as RSX
swizzled surfaces are, goes through the same conversions as a linear one into a temporary linear image, then is
scattered to (or gathered from) guest memory in Morton order. A swizzled target's pitch is its row of texels whatever
the pitch register says (RPCS3 get_framebuffer_layout), so what it covers, and so what overlaps it, is its size.
Swizzled depth buffers are still refused, and logged.
- Run: the first mission as before, one failure (MSAA).
- Test: a red triangle rendered into a 64x64 swizzled target reads back at its Morton addresses; a texel the CPU
  writes there reloads, and the triangle stays.

## D-112 · 2026-10-05 · 16-bit and G8B8 targets write back and reload

R5G6B5 and X1R5G5B5 targets render into BGRA8 copies (8 bits a channel) and G8B8 into RG8 (blue in R, green in G,
RPCS3 color_utils.hpp); their write-back and reload (D-110) refused them. Now R5G6B5 and X1R5G5B5 go to guest memory as
big-endian 16-bit pixels, each channel rounded to 5 or 6 bits, and come back expanded (bits repeated into the low
ones: every 5- and 6-bit value survives the round trip exactly); X1R5G5B5's X bit is one or zero by variant. G8B8 goes
as green then blue. None is used by GTA V's first mission; other games render to them.
- Tests: the four formats round-trip through a CPU write and a reload, the X bit as its variant says.

## D-113 · 2026-10-05 · Vertex programs branch and call on the transform branch bits (BRB, CLB)

BRB and CLB were refused, so a vertex program with them skipped its draws. As RPCS3 (VertexProgramDecompiler
GetOptionalBranchCond): they are taken when bit D3.branch_index (bits 23-27) of NV4097_SET_TRANSFORM_BRANCH_BITS is set,
or, with D3.brb_cond_true (bit 28) clear, when it is clear; the condition codes play no part. BRB jumps, CLB calls (the
call stack CAL uses). The register reaches the shader in the vertex parameters (the spare word after restart_index), set
every draw. Not used by GTA V's first mission; engines branch on these bits between variants of one program.
- Test: one triangle per case, its colour from c[0] or c[1] by a BRB or a CLB on bit 2, taken and not, on a set and on
  a clear bit.

## D-114 · 2026-10-05 · The shader cache: programs and pipelines recorded, then made ahead while the game loads

On the iPhone the game "lags at first, then runs smooth" whenever something new happens: the RSX thread compiled each
new program (newLibraryWithSource) and pipeline (newRenderPipelineStateWithDescriptor) at the draw that first needed
it. Run 082 timed it: the first mission made 558 programs and 497 pipelines, 6.1 s of stalls when it started and
2.3 s in the vault scene on an M4 Mac. The fps dips at its start (12 to 24) were compiles. A phone compiles several times
slower.
- **Recorded**: every program the backend compiles is a file in the cache directory, programs/<hash of its key>.txt,
  holding its key, its translation's entry and masks, its ucode (the collision check) and its MSL source. Every
  pipeline is a line of pipelines.txt: its two program keys and `PipelineParams`, everything else a pipeline is made from
  (formats, write masks, blending), which `pipeline_for` now builds its key and descriptor from.
- **Made ahead**: when the backend starts, two or three background threads (utility QoS) load what is recorded, in the
  directory and in read-only seed directories, then make every program and every pipeline whose two programs they
  made. The RSX thread takes what they made before each program and pipeline lookup. A program it compiled itself
  meanwhile stays; a pipeline joins only with the functions it was made with. Anything new still compiles at its draw,
  and is recorded.
- **Where**: `pspocket-boot --shader-cache DIR`; `translate-game.sh` records into inventory/<TITLE_ID>/shaders (its runs
  now use Metal). `scripts/ios.sh` puts that directory in the app as `shaders`, a seed; the app records into
  Library/Caches/pspocket-shaders. So the phone's first session has the Mac's recording, and later ones their own too.
- Run 082: with the cache, everything was made in 0.4 s while the game loaded (the system's Metal cache helps on the
  Mac); the mission then compiled no program and a few pipelines (about 0.1 ms each), and ran at 28 to 30 fps throughout.
- Also: compile time in the per-frame report; `PSPOCKET_RSX_CHECK_SURFACES`, a diagnostic for textures sampled from
  surfaces whose guest memory changed under them (a write the backend was not told of). It found none in the mission:
  the red and black flashes the iPhone shows are not that, at least there.
- Tests: a second backend on the same cache directory compiles nothing for a draw the first one compiled two programs
  and a pipeline for; the surface check reports a write behind the backend's back.

## D-115 · 2026-10-05 · Conditional rendering draws while its query is still being counted

On the iPhone, parts of characters (whole people, or some of their clothes) flashed black or red now and then.
Conditional rendering (D-102) read the report a query writes when the method ran; occlusion counts arrive only when the
GPU has finished the query's draws, so what it read was an older count. In GTA V every test comes in the frame of its
query, before the frame's work is submitted: all 4,905 to 7,736 draws a run skipped were decided by some earlier
frame's count. A part that had been hidden then was skipped while the passes around it (its depth among them) drew, and
the lighting shaded the hole with what the G-buffer held: black or red. The phone's slower GPU makes the counts later
still.
- The backend now says which report values have a count on its way (`report_pending`: registered by report_zpass,
  counted down by the completion handler that writes them). A test on one of those draws: an older count is no answer.
  RPCS3 evaluates on the GPU instead (VK_EXT_conditional_rendering); Metal has no predicated draws.
- Run 083: no draw skipped by conditional rendering in the first mission (all its tests found their counts pending),
  GPU 8.7 ms a frame at 30 fps, same frames. Occlusion culling by conditional rendering is lost with it; a GPU-side test
  (an indirect draw whose count a compute pass writes from the visibility buffer) would bring it back.
- Also: the app target, not the runtime library, holds the shaders folder (D-114): a library's resources reach no
  bundle, and build 126 went out without the Mac's recording.
- Test: a draw under a report the GPU has not counted renders even though the memory holds zero; once counted, the same
  test skips.

## D-116 · 2026-10-05 · Textures and surfaces unused for a minute are freed

The texture cache only ever grew: an entry went away only when its own memory changed. GTA V streams textures to new
places all the time, and in five minutes of the first mission the cache reached 856 textures, with 153 surfaces next
to them. A Mac does not notice; a phone has a few GB for everything, and a long session would end with the system
closing the app.
- Every texture and surface remembers the flip it was last used in (a texture when bound, a surface when it is a
  target or sampled). Every 150 flips the backend frees the textures unused for `evict_after_flips` flips (1,800 by
  default: a minute at 30 fps; one used again is decoded again from memory), and the surfaces unused as long whose
  guest memory holds what they do (not newer on the GPU, not a target of the open pass or the draw).
- The per-frame report shows both caches' sizes.
- Run: the cache now goes up and down with the scene (268 to 663 textures over five minutes), surfaces about 150
  (44 MB); same frames.
- Test: a texture unused for a few flips (the limit set low) is freed, then decoded again when a draw uses it.

## D-117 · 2026-10-05 · The phone records what the translation does not cover, for the Mac to pull

The user plays further on the phone than the Mac's scripted runs reach, and SPU code the translation has not reached
runs in the interpreter there, slowly. The app now keeps what it meets, the way pspocket-boot keeps it on the Mac:
- SPU programs without a lifted program are saved, with their seeds (`hle::set_spu_dump_dir`), and every address lifted
  code did not reach is appended to a miss log in the log's own words (`ps_spu_set_miss_log`, new), in
  Library/Application Support/pspocket-coverage (kept by the system, not shown in Files). Shaders already went to
  Library/Caches/pspocket-shaders (D-114).
- `scripts/ios.sh pull-coverage` copies both from the phone (devicectl; `PSPOCKET_PULL_FROM` takes a container on this
  Mac, a simulator's) into the game's inventory directory: new programs, new seed lines, the misses as a run log
  (run-phone-<time>.log, which scripts/lift-spu.sh and translate-game.sh read), new shaders and pipelines. The next
  lift and build cover what the phone met.
- Tests: a miss reaches the miss log in the words lift-spu.sh matches; the merge, on a fake container.

## D-118 · 2026-10-05 · A FIFO desync is reported in full and read again; the phone's records are per game

The phone froze when the player switched to Trevor (the prologue's first switch, past the Mac's scripted runs). Its
log: three `BEGIN_END` arguments that were the next method's header (0x41710: the reader one word out of step, then
back), and a few minutes later, twelve words after a jump to a new 8 KB stretch of the command buffer, a header for
method 0x0080 with 32 arguments that are good commands, then a malformed word. The recovery skipped to put, 480 KB on,
past label writes the game waits for, so it hung. Run 049 and a Mac walk (invalid primitive 36) showed the same signs.
Neither log says which word the reader took wrong, so:
- The reader keeps the last 256 words it read. A desync (a malformed word, a method no class defines, an impossible
  primitive) is reported with them, oldest first, each beside what memory holds now where that differs: a changed
  word was read before the guest finished writing it; an unchanged run shows a misread of good commands. The words
  after the point come too. A few reports per run.
- A desync within 16384 words of a jump, call or return goes back to its target a millisecond later and reads the
  stretch again, twice at most per target; then the old recovery. During the re-read the semaphore acquires the reader
  passed before the desync point hold (their semaphores may have moved on, and waiting again would hang); past the
  point, and after any jump, they wait again. Commands before the point run twice (state, the odd draw, label writes
  of the same values), which is better than a hang. Dev runs without `--rsx-recover` still stop at the error.
- The phone keeps its shader cache and coverage per game, in folders named by the disc's title ID, and uses the
  shaders recorded on the Mac only for the game whose translated code the app holds: the user also boots other games
  (Assassin's Creed) in the test app. `scripts/ios.sh pull-coverage` takes only the game's folders (its title ID from
  `<game>/title-id` or the directory's name); the shared folder of builds up to 131 only with
  `PSPOCKET_PULL_SHARED=1`.
- Tests: a stretch written after it was first read is read again; a stretch that stays wrong is read three times and
  then skipped to put; an acquire passed before the desync holds during the re-read and waits again past it.

## D-119 · 2026-10-05 · A clear writes its value into A8B8G8R8 targets as it is (red and blue trade places)

On the iPhone characters, or parts of their clothes, flashed fully red or black (run 084 reproduced it on the Mac:
every frame of the bank walk saved, scanned for red and black bumps, then frame traces). The red: GTA V draws its
characters with a damage target (A8B8G8R8, at 0xcf3f0000) that it clears every frame to 0x00ff0000 and samples as
A8R8G8B8: transparent red, no damage. The clear value is A8R8G8B8, and the RSX writes it into the pixel's word as it
is; an A8B8G8R8 target's RGBA8Unorm copy holds r g b a, so the value's red byte is its blue. The backend took the value
as red, green, blue: to the texture it was transparent blue, and the clothes it touched came out red. Now red and blue
trade places in the value and in the clear's channel mask for A8B8G8R8 and X8B8G8R8 targets (RPCS3 VKGSRender.cpp
clear_surface, get_abgr8_clear_color, get_abgr8_clearmask). Draws need nothing: the shader's outputs land as r g b a.
- The frame trace saves every 2D texture a traced frame samples as `trace-N/tex-<address>-fmt<format>-t<unit>-WxH.png`,
  as the shader sees it, and prints each target's pitch. `pspocket-boot --frame-from N` saves frames from N on; frames
  are written on threads of their own, so saving every frame keeps 30 fps.
- Test: a clear of 0x11223344 reads back from an A8B8G8R8 target as those bytes, and a clear of only the red channel
  writes the value's red byte.

## D-120 · 2026-10-05 · A target narrower than the one at its address is its corner; a wider one keeps what it held

The black flashes: GTA V clears the right half of that damage target as 2560x512, then draws into its left half as a
1280x512 target with the same pitch, and samples it as 2560x512. A surface was found only by address, size, pitch and
format, so the narrow one evicted the wide one and its cleared half was gone; the 2560-wide texture sampled the
1280-wide surface stretched, and the characters came out black. Its 1280x720 depth buffer, used at 1280x512 by the
same pass, was made anew each frame the same way.
- A colour target at the start of a larger one with its pitch and format, or a depth buffer at the start of a larger
  one, is that surface: the pass draws in its top-left corner, the surface clip (`PassTargets::width, height`, the
  descriptor's render target size). Its load-action clear would clear the whole attachment, so such a pass clears
  with a quad.
- A larger colour target over a smaller one at its start takes guest memory, then the smaller one's pixels in its
  corner (`grow_surface`), instead of starting empty.
- A texture smaller than the target at its address, with its pitch, samples a copy of the target's top-left corner,
  made again when the target changes (`Surface::corners`). A larger one (an MSAA target read at its sample layout)
  still samples it stretched.
- Tests: a narrow target keeps the wide one's other half; a wide one keeps the narrow one's pixels; a texture of half
  the width samples only the left half.
- Run 084: the robber who turned black then red keeps his green jacket and red and teal hat. Not yet: the security
  guard in the hostage cutscene still turns black at the cut to his close-up. The 640x256 target GTA V clears at
  0xcf670000 (pitch 0x2800) lies inside the 2560x512 one, 256 rows down, and evicts it, decals and all: the guard's
  texture then decodes the stale memory under it. Targets inside other targets at any offset come next.

## D-121 · 2026-10-05 · The phone decrypts a disc's executable itself; so does the Mac's factory

The user picked Assassin's Creed (BLES00158) on the phone and the app said its decrypted EBOOT was not there: until
now an executable was decrypted on the Mac (RPCS3, or the firmware script of D-046) and pushed with `scripts/ios.sh
push-game`. The user wants any disc picked on the phone to boot ("the decryption should run inside the iPhone"), so
the keys now travel in the app, never in the repository (CLAUDE.md rule 1), and D-071's "keys never go into the app"
is replaced.
- `recomp::decrypt_self` (recomp/common/src/self_decrypt.cpp) follows RPCS3's SELFDecrypter (Crypto/unself.cpp):
  the metadata info opens with the AES-256-CBC key of the executable's type and key revision (KeyVault::FindSelfKey),
  the metadata with the AES-128-CTR key and counter inside it, each segment with its own; zlib segments inflate; the
  ELF is laid out from the SELF's plain copies of its headers. CommonCrypto (Apple platforms) and the system zlib.
  Debug SELFs give their plain ELF; PSN executables (an NPDRM control header) need their licence and are refused.
- The keys: `scripts/self-keys.py` reads RPCS3's Crypto/key_vault.cpp at build time (`PSPOCKET_RPCS3_DIR`, by default
  the checkout beside this one) into `build/host/recomp/common/generated/self_keys.cpp`, which the host build and the
  iOS app compile. Without RPCS3's source the table is empty and decrypting says so. The script never prints a key.
- `ps_disc_decrypt_executable` reads PS3_GAME/USRDIR/EBOOT.BIN from the disc image and writes the ELF (whole or not
  at all). Its folder is made from the deepest one that exists: on the phone `create_directories` did not make
  game/BLES00158/ (iOS's sandbox does not let the app look above its container), and the first try said "cannot
  write"; errors now carry the system's reason. The app calls it when a disc is picked and Documents/game/<TITLE_ID>/EBOOT.elf is missing, showing
  "Decrypting the game's EBOOT.BIN"; `ps3disc --decrypt IMAGE OUT.elf` on the Mac; `scripts/translate-game.sh` no
  longer needs `--elf`.
- Check: GTA V's EBOOT.BIN decrypts in 0.4 s to an ELF byte for byte the one decrypted before (sha-256 8cad8baa...);
  Assassin's Creed's to a 20.7 MB PPU executable.
- Tests: a synthetic executable compressed and encrypted with made-up keys as a retail SELF is comes back out; a missing
  key, a wrong key, an empty table and a PSN executable are refused with the reason; FindSelfKey's choices; a debug
  SELF. A game without its translated code boots in the interpreters: slow, but it boots.

## D-122 · 2026-10-05 · A target inside a larger one is its child: both kept, each sees what the other wrote

The black security guard of run 084 (D-120's last open case): GTA V clears a 640x256 target 256 rows into its
2560x512 damage target (0xcf670000 inside 0xcf3f0000, the same pitch 0x2800), and the guard's draws sample the large
one. A new surface for the small one evicted the large one, decals and all; the guard's texture then decoded the
stale memory under it. A target that lies inside a larger colour target with its pitch and format, not at its start
(that is D-120's corner), is now its child (`Surface::parent`, `children`):
- It keeps its own texture: a pass with it has its depth buffer at its own origin, which drawing into the parent's
  texture at an offset could not give (Metal offsets every attachment together). The parent stays.
- What one writes reaches the other on the GPU, before the other is used (`sync_surface`: drawn to, sampled, read
  back, copied): a child's pixels go into its place in the parent; after the parent is written, the child takes its
  place back (`surface_written`). A child that goes leaves its pixels in its parent; children of a parent that goes
  stand alone.
- Test: a child cleared inside a cleared parent: the parent sampled as a texture shows the child where it lies and
  itself beside it, and reads back so; the parent written over part of the child, then the child drawn again: the
  child had taken its place back first.

## D-123 · 2026-10-05 · A FIFO reset stops the reader before its next word

`sys_rsx_context_attribute(0x001)` sets get and put. The RSX applied it at the start of its next batch (up to 4096
words), and in the meantime read on at the old get against the new put: past the old put's stretch, into stale
words, which it executed until the batch ended (a stale label write is enough to hang the game). Now the reset is
flagged first and put published after it with a release store, and the reader checks the flag after each read of
put: a reader that sees the new put stops before reading a word at the old get. Each reset is logged ("FIFO set").
In the Mac's first-mission walk GTA V does not reset the FIFO; whether it does at the iPhone's freeze (the switch to
Trevor) the next phone log shows.
- Test: the game moves the FIFO at the first clear of a stream of three: the other two never run.

## D-124 · 2026-10-05 · An SPU PUT writes its first word last: the RSX resumes only on a whole block

The iPhone's FIFO desyncs (several a minute in the first mission's escape; D-118's reports show them): the RSX parked
on a jump-to-self, the word changed, and the words after it were the previous lap's: the first eight new, the rest
stale, overwritten moments later. A probe of every SPU DMA into the command ring (100,000 in a Mac run of the
mission) showed how GTA V fills it: its graphics jobs (two programs, three PUT sites) write each block of RSX
commands, 16 bytes to 4.5 KB, with one PUT, whose first word lands over the jump-to-self the RSX waits on. A plain copy's
stores reach another core in any order on ARM, and the SPU thread can be preempted inside it; on the Cell the block
lands long before the RSX looks again. Every PUT longer than a word now copies all but its first word, then stores the
first word with release: the RSX's acquire load of the parked word sees the whole block (D-077's release fence before
each PUT still orders PUTs among themselves). D-118's re-read stays as the net under it. The app's frame-rate line now
also says iOS's heat level ("heat nominal / fair / serious / critical").
- No test reproduces the race without the game: it lives in the order stores reach another core.

## D-125 · 2026-10-05 · A job chain command with the JTS bit waits, whatever its low word

The iPhone stopped in the first mission's escape on "job descriptor: 0x280 bytes at 0x8102db800 are not in guest
memory": a job chain (workload 11) took 0x00000008_102db800 as a JOB at a 36-bit address. The descriptor at
0x102db800 was whole; the high word was a JTS's (0x00000008_00000012, RPCS3's CELL_SPURS_JOB_OPCODE_JTS). The PPU
rewrites a JTS into a JOB low word first, then the high word: between the two stores the command keeps the JTS bit,
and libsre reads it as a jump to self until the high word lands. Only the whole JTS value waited here. Now any command
with bit 35 (the JTS bit) ends the batch with pc unchanged, as a JTS does.
- Test: a chain whose second command is a JOB's low word over a JTS waits on its SPU; once the high word is written
  the job runs (without the change it stops on the phone's MFC fault).

## D-126 · 2026-10-05 · cellSysmoduleSetMemcontainer: a container is checked and remembered

The iPhone stopped after 15 minutes of the first mission: GTA V called cellSysmoduleSetMemcontainer (unimplemented,
an error) with a memory container it had made, then trapped on its own assertion (tw 31,r1,r1 at 0xa3a16c). Now it
follows RPCS3: SYS_MEMORY_CONTAINER_ID_INVALID returns to no container; any other ID must be a memory container with
0x60000 bytes free (sys_memory_container_get_size), or CELL_SYSMODULE_ERROR_INVALID_MEMCONTAINER. The container would
hold the PRX images of later loads; HLE modules have none, so it is only remembered.
- Test: a fresh 1 MB container, no container, a wrong ID, and a container with 64 KB left.

## D-127 · 2026-10-05 · Translated SPU calls save only what the callee can touch; byte rotates and cflts in NEON

A 10 s Time Profiler recording of the iPhone in the first mission's escape (heat "serious", 9 to 17 fps): the process
used 5.8 of the phone's 6 cores, 4.6 of them the six SPU workers, 79% of that in translated SPU code. A quarter of
the translated code's time was the register saves and reloads around its own calls: each call stored every register
the caller writes and reloaded every register it uses (up to 127 of each), though GTA V's jobs call small helpers
from large functions. Now spu-lift works out, for each function and everything it calls, the registers it may read
or write through ctx (its entry loads what it uses, its exits store what it writes); a call stores only what the
caller wrote of the callee's set and reloads only what it uses of what the callee may write. A callee that does not
come back to the call (it left for the run loop) has the caller store the rest of what it wrote before returning:
each caller up the chain does the same, so ctx is whole again for the run loop. A stop (its handlers read and write
any register) or a call through a register touches everything, as before.

Two helpers were most of the rest: rotqby's 128-bit integer rotate moved the value through general registers (6
instructions for an immediate count, about 30 and a branch for a register count) and is now one EXT or TBL for an
immediate (shlqbyi, rotqbyi, rotqmbyi as constant shuffles) and a TBL for a register count; cflts and cfltu went
through double precision lane by lane and are now FCVTZS/FCVTZU on the power-of-two-scaled lanes, with exponent 0
giving 0 and exponent 255 saturating by sign (checked against the old form over every scale and edge values: 16.6
million lanes, no difference).
- Measured (run 085, the Mac's walk of run 080, 20 s at 30 fps): translated SPU code 14.8 s to 12.7 s (-14%), the
  saves 2.20 s to 1.66 s, the reloads 2.74 s to 2.24 s; what is left of them is mostly each function's own entry
  loads and exit stores.
- Test: the program-level fuzz program keeps registers across a call that does not touch them, has them read and
  written by the callee, written two calls deep, and kept across a call that leaves the program and comes back
  through the run loop (without the early-exit stores, or without the reload, it fails).

## D-128 · 2026-10-05 · SPU channels of the SPU's own state without the lock; the timebase by one multiply

The same iPhone recording: the SPU workers spent 1.2 s of 10 s in the channel lock's mutex, and 1.1 s reading the
clock for SPU_RdDec: GTA V's jobs read the decrementer millions of times a second, and ps_timebase_now did two
128-bit divisions each time. Channels whose state only the SPU's own thread writes (SRR0, the event and tag masks,
the machine status, the decrementer, and a DMA's parameters: LSA, EAH, EAL, size, tag, the command) no longer take
the lock (mfc_command already took its own where it needs one). The timebase is the host ticks times a 32.32
fixed-point factor (79.8 MHz over the host's 24 MHz on Apple silicon): one multiply, drifting about a microsecond a
day, monotonic.

## D-130 · 2026-10-05 · A line snapshot reads the line twice: a plain writer's stores are seen in their order

The iPhone stopped a minute into the first mission with the new build (D-127 to D-129): the EDGE/GFX job chain took
a JOB whose descriptor at 0x102f5e00 held vertex-like data and failed with CELL_SPURS_JOB_ERROR_NUM_CACHE (the chain
halts on errors). The PPU appends commands with plain stores: the new commands, lwsync, then the word over the
jump-to-self that publishes them. The job chain reads its 16 commands with ps_res_acquire, whose seqlock catches
conditional stores only; its 16 loads are not ordered among themselves, so it could take the new first command next
to the previous lap's commands after it, a JOB of a descriptor slot since reused. The Cell's GETLLAR reads the line
whole. Now ps_res_acquire reads the line again after its acquire fence and retries until both reads agree: a store
the first read saw has every store its writer ordered before it visible to the second. Plain GETs end with an
acquire fence for the same reason: an SPU that GETs a flag and then the data it announces reads them in that order.
- Test: a writer fills a line (the data, a release fence, then the flag word, at either end of the line) while
  snapshots are taken: none may hold the flag's value next to an older value of the data. Without the second read it
  fails at both ends on the M4 (the loads do reorder).

## D-134 · 2026-10-05 · Textures are watched by page protection, and a store beside one keeps it

The iPhone's RSX thread hashed 75 to 85 MB of texture memory a frame (about 1,100 checks), a fifth of its time and a

## D-136 · 2026-10-05 · Job chains and tasksets are shut down and joined natively

GTA V imports cellSpursShutdownJobChain, cellSpursJoinJobChain and cellSpursJoinTaskset, and a call would have
stopped the game as unimplemented. They follow RPCS3 (cellSpurs.cpp): the shutdown is cellSpursShutdownWorkload on
the chain's workload; a join waits for the workload's shutdown, removes the workload (state NON_EXISTENT, its enabled
and mskB bits cleared, the workload flag released if it had it), sets the chain's workload ID to 32 and returns the
chain's error word. RPCS3 leaves cellSpursJoinTaskset empty; here it waits and removes like the chain's join, so the
game may free the taskset after it.
- The native wait is for more than the state: no worker inside the workload (a count per workload in the scheduler)
  and none still counted in its contention. The game frees the chain or taskset once a join returns, and a worker
  could still be in its last job.
- A worker selects from states read before its update of the contention line, so a shutdown and a join can come in
  between. It now counts itself inside, then reads the state again, both sequentially consistent, as the join reads
  the state and then the count: either the worker sees the shutdown and leaves, or the join sees the worker and
  waits. A worker that picked a slot just before its join removed it gives the contention back at its next selection;
  adding a workload waits for that (up to a second) instead of stopping on RPCS3's check.
- A job chain that stops on an error shuts its workload down from the SPU (SHUTTING_DOWN), and no system service
  makes it removable natively. The join does that step once the last worker left, with the completion bit in the
  workload's event byte, as RPCS3's spursSysServiceUpdateWorkload does.
- Tests: a chain shut down and joined frees its slot, which a new chain gets and runs; argument errors and the
  instance's exception state; a join waits for the job still running at the shutdown; a chain halted by an unknown
  command is joined and the join returns the error. The taskset's join gets the same checks.

## D-137 · 2026-10-05 · A texture over a render target of another format: the target laid over memory on the GPU; G8B8

On the iPhone the frame rate fell to 2 to 4 fps where GTA V reads its 640x360 F_W16Z16Y16X16 target as a 1280x720
A8R8G8B8 texture: each time the target went to guest memory first (D-080), a readback the RSX thread waits for (270 in
one session), with the phone's GPU a frame behind. The other common readback in the phone's logs (325 to 463 a
session) was a 256x256 G8B8 target read as a G8B8 texture, a format the decoder did not have: the draw failed after
the wait anyway.
- A texture of another format over a target the GPU drew since memory last held it is now decoded from a copy of
  guest memory over which a compute kernel first writes the target's pixels as store_readback lays them in memory
  (rsx_*_to_memory: the 8-bit formats from their unorm channels, the float ones through an integer view so their
  bits pass as they are, Z24S8 and Z16 depth buffers), on the render buffer after the passes that drew it. Guest
  memory is not written. The cached texture keeps the target's serial (never reused) and generations, and is decoded
  again when the target is drawn to again or another target, or none, is newer there.
  MetalBackendConfig::overlay_targets (PSPOCKET_RSX_WRITE_BACK_TARGETS) returns to the write-back.
- G8B8 textures decode as RPCS3 uploads them (the big-endian halfword into R8G8: red the B byte, green the G byte) and
  read (A, R, G, B) = (G, B, G, B), RPCS3's mapping; a G8B8 texture over a G8B8 target samples the target, whose RG8
  copy holds the same.
- The tests found a target whose open pass had only a clear so far laid over before the clear ran: a load action runs
  with its pass and counts in the generation then. bind_texture now runs such a pass before reading its target.
- Measured (Mac, run 080's walk with --gpu metal): readbacks the RSX thread waited for, 42 in the walk (0.09 to 0.16 ms
  a frame) before, 0 after; "G8B8 is not decoded yet" gone. The phone's numbers come with its next build.
- Tests: a float16 target read as an A8R8G8B8 texture twice as wide and twice as tall (its lower half memory) gives
  the same pixels laid over as written back, without a readback; laid over again after the target is cleared, the
  clear seen; a Z24S8 buffer read as R5G6B5 of another size likewise; a G8B8 target sampled and G8B8 memory decoded;
  G8B8 in the GPU against CPU decode comparison.

## D-141 · 2026-10-05 · sys_net offline, with loopback between the game's own sockets; cellHttp and cellSsl

The last of GTA V's 113 unimplemented imports: 23 sys_net functions, 6 cellHttp, 3 cellSsl. Online play is a non-goal
(D-024): no traffic leaves the process. RPCS3's checks, errno values and structure layouts are kept (sys_net.cpp,
lv2/sys_net.cpp, cellHttp.cpp, cellSsl.cpp).
- Sockets are numbered as RPCS3's (24 to 1023, then the lowest free, then EMFILE); errors set the thread's errno where
  RPCS3 puts it (r13 - 0x7030 + 0x2c) and return -1.
- Only 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1 and multicast bind; any address outside 127/8 is EADDRNOTAVAIL (RPCS3's answer with its
  network disconnected). Between the game's own sockets UDP and TCP work in memory, with BSD's EOF, EPIPE and buffer
  limits; nobody listening is ECONNREFUSED.
- A blocking recv, recvfrom or accept without a timeout waits as on a console without a link (its receive thread parks)
  until data, a shutdown, a close from another thread (EINTR, as RPCS3), SO_RCVTIMEO (EWOULDBLOCK) or the process
  end: an invented error could send such a thread into a loop that takes a core on the phone. The first wait on each
  socket is logged, and it shows in the thread report.
- gethostbyname answers dotted addresses and fails names with TRY_AGAIN; select counts sockets and never sets
  exceptfds; socket info reports the real queued bytes (RPCS3 reports 0).
- cellHttp and cellSsl: RPCS3's init and end state machines; cellSslCertificateLoader answers as RPCS3 with no
  firmware certificates installed (size 0, or zeros).
- Guesses where the PS3's own behaviour is not known: ephemeral ports from 49152, a backlog cap of 128, EOF (not a
  reset) for a socket closed with unread data, ECONNREFUSED for a full backlog; sys_net_get_sockinfo_ex's fourth
  argument taken as flags.

## D-143 · 2026-10-05 · The shader cache makes pipelines first, in first-use order, on half the cores; the iPhone keeps their GPU code in binary archives

On the iPhone the first minutes of play ran at 4 to 10 fps (run 087): the cache (D-114, D-118) compiled all of its
~7,500 programs before the first of its ~11,600 pipelines, on two threads at utility QoS (iOS runs those on the
efficiency cores), so no pipeline the game needed was ready when play began and the RSX thread compiled 821 itself in
the first 300 frames. And every launch compiled everything again.
- **Order:** pipelines as pipelines.txt lists them (the order the game first needed them), each with its two programs
  compiled on demand, once (a worker that needs a program another is compiling waits for it); then the programs no
  pipeline names.
- **Threads:** half the cores, 2 to 4 (3 on the iPhone's 6), at user-initiated QoS while the game loads; each drops
  to utility after 45 s, when the game is playing (three threads at user-initiated QoS left the iPhone's sound at
  half speed).
- **GPU binary archives (the iPhone app only, `shader_archives`):** each worker adds what it compiles to its own
  MTLBinaryArchive and writes it to the cache directory (archive-<launch>-<worker>.bin, every 400 pipelines and at the
  end); the next launch loads them all and makes its pipelines from them (MTLPipelineOptionFailOnBinaryArchiveMiss),
  compiling only the misses, and the RSX thread's own pipelines look there too. An archive that does not load (an OS
  update) is deleted. Pipelines that write no colour are left out: an archive holding one is not saved ("expecting
  'fragment' stage in pipeline").
- **Measured on the iPhone 17 Pro Max:** 10,000 of 11,634 pipelines ready when play began, 45 compiled on the RSX
  thread in the first 300 frames (17 to 23 fps, run 087); the next boots were done in 43 and 41 s and held 30 fps
  until play (run 088).
- **Open:** the iPhone's archive saves still report "expecting 'fragment' stage" or "missing 'vertex' stage in
  pipeline no. N" and keep only part of what was added: 3,623 of 11,756 pipelines came from the archives in the
  second boot, 5,307 of 11,770 in the third. The Mac saves every kind of pipeline tried (run 088).

## D-144 · 2026-10-05 · Write tracking: a page's protection changes only in states the other threads wait out

GTA V's screen flickered with other textures' colours on the iPhone and the Mac from D-134 on (13:38; "the game ran
good this morning"). The Mac walk counted 215 to 322 jumps in its frames with page protection, 2 (camera cuts) with
textures hashed instead (run 088).
- **The race:** a fault marked its page resolved and then made it writable with an mprotect; check() could make the
  page read-only again in between, and the fault's mprotect landed after: the page stayed writable while the tracker
  took it for protected, and every later store into it went unseen until something else dirtied the texture. GTA V's
  threads store beside its textures all the time (16 KB pages), so this happened many times a minute.
- **The fix:** each page has a state: unprotected (never protected), protecting, protected, resolving, resolved,
  releasing, released. Every mprotect happens in one of the three transitional states, entered by compare-and-swap
  and left by the thread that entered it; whoever meets one waits for it to end (an mprotect, microseconds). So the
  state always says what the page's protection is, and a fault handled late (its store faulted while the page was
  protected) sees what happened since: protected again, it is resolved again (harmless); released, the store is
  retried, up to 1,024 times per release so that a fault that is not ours still reaches the crash handler; a page
  freed since is never retried. One thread (the RSX thread) watches, checks and unwatches; any thread may fault.
- **Test:** three threads store beside a watched range while the main thread checks it, stores into it, checks
  again, unwatches it and watches it again, 50,000 times: every store into it must be seen and every fault handled.
  The D-134 code crashes it (SIGBUS) 3 times in 3; the first fix (the resolving state alone) still crashed it, a
  store faulting while unwatch() released the page; this one passes.
- **Mac walk:** 2 jumps in 829 frames (camera cuts), 37 write faults per frame, 30 fps.

  stops it (os_proc_available_memory): a stop for memory is seen coming in the log.
- **The next boot (17:13):** no memory warnings; 0.86 GB at the loading screens, 1.6 GB in play, with about 6.4 GB
  allowed. The cache made all 13,067 pipelines in 30 s, where the boots with archives took 41 to 43 s: iOS keeps
  the pipelines it compiled for the app between launches itself. The user confirmed the flicker gone (D-144).

## D-147 · 2026-10-05 · Route B: the iPhone translates any game itself, once per game; supersedes D-036 and D-090

The user's goal is any PS3 disc image picked on the iPhone, played with no Mac and no rebuild per game. Until now the
design was one Mac-side build per game (D-036, D-090: the lifters write C, Xcode compiles it into the app). After
Assassin's Creed (BLES00158) failed on the phone while GTA V (BLES01807) runs, the user rejected that as the answer for
"any ISO" (2026-10-05) and chose route B over route A (JIT while playing, through a debugger-attach JIT enabler such
as StikDebug), which stays the fallback if B proves impossible.
- **The flow:** install pspocket once; pick PS3UPDAT.PUP (the user's own download from Sony) once; pick a game. The
  first time, "Preparing game…": the phone decrypts the EBOOT (D-121), runs the lifters, compiles their output to
  ARM64, links it into a library, signs it with the user's development certificate and saves it; then the game boots
  with that library loaded (dlopen). Later launches load the saved library. Code met only at run time (SPU programs,
  mostly) runs in the interpreters, is recorded (D-117) and translated in the background for the next launch.
- **What stays (most of the code):** the runtime (rsx, lv2, spu, ppu with the interpreters as oracle and fallback,
  hle, native SPURS of D-037), recomp/common, the lifters and their analysis, the app. The Mac path (`ppu-lift`,
  `scripts/translate-game.sh`, `PSPOCKET_GAME_PPU/SPU`) stays as the developer's tool, and GTA V's Mac-translated build
  keeps working throughout.
- **What is new:** the translation as a per-game file loaded at run time; code generation on the phone; signing on the
  phone; firmware from the PUP with the real firmware modules (LLE) for what the HLE does not implement; the coverage
  loop on the phone.
- **Stages,** each ending with tests, a commit, a decision and a run note: 1 a go/no-go test (a tiny ARM64 library the
  app writes, signs and loads, for a development install and for TestFlight; if both fail, stop and take route A);
  2 code generation chosen by measurement (embedded LLVM compiling the lifters' C, or a direct ARM64 emitter); 3 the
  translation as a library, on the Mac first; 4 the on-phone pipeline; 5 firmware and PRX loading; 6 acceptance
  (Assassin's Creed to its title screen and GTA V to the prologue's bank, both prepared on the phone).
- **The bar:** each game is rated against "Flawless" (its own frame rate for a full session, PS3-accurate graphics,
  sound in time, saves that persist, an hour with no crash) in docs/compatibility.md: Flawless, Playable, Boots or
  Broken; GTA V and every Flawless game are re-checked after each change (the gate, D-149).
- Rule 1 holds: translated code, decrypted executables, firmware and logs stay on the phone or in inventory/. The
  development certificate's key is the user's own and goes to their phone only, never into the repository.

## D-148 · 2026-10-05 · Feedback copies made once per write, frames in flight capped, GPU caches trimmed when iOS warns

The iPhone stopped GTA V after ten minutes of play (run 089): memory went from 1.8 GB to 4.3 GB and back, then to
4.7 GB, and iOS ended the app. A draw that samples a render target it also draws to got a new full-size copy of the
target every time (3.7 to 14.7 MB), and every copy lived until the GPU had run the frame, with nothing limiting how
many frames the RSX thread queued: about 200 copies a frame in the heavy stretches. GTA V's draws of this kind write
nothing to the target they sample (colour mask 0 there).
- **Feedback copies:** one per surface, made again only after a write to it (its generation; a draw changes it only
  where its mask writes, metal_backend.mm:1204). A new copy is a new texture, as corner copies stay too: copying into
  the one earlier draws read would make the GPU wait for them. GTA V's walk: 5 copies a frame where there were 9 to 16
  target copies, render passes 84 a frame where there were 87, GPU memory flat at 220 to 230 MB.
- **Frames in flight:** at most three (a semaphore the frame's last command buffer signals when it completes); a flip
  waits for the oldest, and the wait is reported per frame (0 ms on the Mac walk: the GPU keeps up there).
- **Transient budget:** past 256 MB of uploads in the command buffer being recorded, it is submitted early.
- **iOS:** on a memory warning, or under 1.5 GB left before iOS stops the app, `MetalBackend::trim_memory()` frees, at
  the next flip, textures and surfaces unused for 60 flips and the feedback copies, and lets finished readbacks land;
  logged. The game's previous log stays as game-prev.log.
- **Telemetry:** the per-frame line tells the five kinds of copies between targets apart (gpu copy, feedback copy,
  corner copy, region copy, grow), and adds the feedback copies, corner textures and surface reloads per frame, the wait
  for the GPU, `MTLDevice.currentAllocatedSize` and the deferred queue; the numbers also go to a callback
  (`MetalBackendConfig::on_window`) for pspocket-boot's summary.
- Tests: 50 draws that sample their own target with the mask off share one copy and one pass; a draw after a write to
  the target samples the write (an old copy would show the clear).

## D-150 · 2026-10-05 · Route B's go/no-go: GO for development installs. The app writes, signs and runs its own code

Route B (D-147) stands or falls on one question: does iOS map code into the app that was signed after the app was
installed? Research (LiveContainer's iOS 26 mode, Apple's TN3125/TN3126, XNU's checks) says: very likely yes for a
development install, with the exact certificate the installed profile lists, the app's team ID in the signature and
Developer Mode on; no for TestFlight (Apple re-signs the app, and no developer profile vouches for the certificate).
- **runtime/codesign (new):** a Mach-O writer for a minimal arm64 library made from bytes (`answer_dylib`: one exported
  function, `mov w0, #42; ret`, an export trie, `LC_BUILD_VERSION`, `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE`), and a signer for any 64-bit
  Mach-O that has a signature load command: a CodeDirectory (version 0x20400, SHA-256 over 4 KB pages, the team ID, the
  exec segment), the designated requirement codesign and zsign write for a development certificate, and a detached CMS
  SignedData (content type data, the certificate chain, the CDHashes and CDHashes2 attributes) in our own DER, signed
  with RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 SHA-256 through Security.framework. No OpenSSL (zsign's is GPL-incompatible); zsign, ChOma (MIT)
  and Apple's tools were the reference, nothing copied from ldid or LiveContainer (AGPL).
- **Checked on the Mac:** Apple's `codesign --verify` accepts the ad hoc signature and the library loads and returns 42;
  with an identity, codesign reads the team, identifier, CodeDirectory hash and requirement back, and Security.framework's
  CMS decoder verifies the signature over the CodeDirectory (tests/codesign). `pspocket-codesign` makes and signs
  libraries on the Mac and exports the Apple Development identity for the phone (`scripts/ios.sh
  push-signing-identity`: a .p12 under a random password, with its chain; the key is the user's own and never committed).
- **The probe:** `codegen.dlopen` in the self-test loads every library in Library/Application Support/pspocket-codegen
  the way LiveContainer does (a fresh copy, `F_ADDFILESIGS_RETURN` with the signature's place, `F_CHECK_LV`, dlopen,
  dlsym, call) and, with the identity there, writes and signs a library itself and loads that. `scripts/codegen-probe.sh`
  builds the variants (clang-built and ours, signed by codesign with the app's bundle ID or the default identifier),
  copies them to the phone, runs the self-test and prints what iOS said.
- **Result on the iPhone 17 Pro Max, iOS 26, development install (run 091): 4 of 4 libraries ran.** All three signed on
  the Mac by codesign (both identifiers, and our own Mach-O) and the one the app wrote and signed itself on the phone
  (team M7XJA39ZV6, the chain WWDR + Apple Root CA): signature registered, library validation passed, dlopen, ps_answer()
  = 42. Route B goes ahead; games are delivered to the phone by cable or Xcode installs (the development profile), where
  the app signs what it translates. TestFlight (1c) is checked next; the research expects it to fail.

## D-151 · 2026-10-05 · Route B's code generator: LLVM's clang and lld inside the app, compiling the lifters' C

Stage 2 of route B (D-147): how the phone turns a game's code into ARM64. Two candidates: compile the C the lifters
already write, with LLVM inside the app, or a new emitter from the lifters' IR straight to ARM64 (about 650 instruction
forms, each with its own differential fuzz test under rule 3). Measured (runs 091, 092), LLVM wins on every count that
matters now: it reuses the lifters and their fuzz tests unchanged, its code is the code the Mac builds and the gate
checks, and the phone compiles fast enough.
- **runtime/codegen (new):** `compile_c` runs clang's front end and AArch64 back end in process (iOS starts no other
  programs) and `link_dylib` runs lld's Mach-O linker; LLVM 22.1.8 (RPCS3's copy) as static libraries,
  `scripts/build-llvm-ios.sh` (AArch64 only, no tools). The phone has no SDK: the code compiles against clang's own
  headers (3.3 MB of them, bundled in the app's codegen folder), `runtime/codegen/sysroot` (our own string.h, math.h and
  a libSystem.tbd naming the symbols translated code calls) and the runtime's ABI headers. Flags as the builds':
  -O2 (-O1 is no faster and no smaller), `-ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math`, no stack protector.
- **In process, unlike clang:** each compile on its own thread with clang's 8 MB stack (iOS gives threads 512 KB);
  `DisableFree` off (the driver's `-disable-free` leaked each compile's AST and module); freed pages returned to iOS
  after each compile (`malloc_zone_pressure_relief`); the compile job taken from clang's driver as `clang -c -o` makes
  it (`clang::createInvocation` adds `-fsyntax-only`, which drops `-o`); lld asked for the signature's room
  (`-adhoc_codesign`: it reserves one unasked only for macOS), which runtime/codesign then fills (D-150). LLVM's own
  options (`-mllvm`) through `set_llvm_options`, process-wide, before compiles start.
- **On the iPhone 17 Pro Max:** C compiled, linked, signed and loaded by the app, all on the phone (50 ms for a small
  program). GTA V's code compiles as fast per core as on the M4: a 1.8 MB PPU unit in 1.6 s, its slowest SPU programs in
  35-38 s; six compiles at once give 2.35 MB of C a second; 155 s of full load left the phone nominal. LLVM adds 66 MB
  to the app's code.
- **GTA V, one of the biggest PS3 executables, is about 14 minutes today** (823 MB of PPU C and 86 MB of SPU C; all of
  it takes 8 minutes on the M4's ten cores with `pspocket-cc`, the same compiler as a Mac command). Where it goes and
  what cuts it, to be measured against the game's speed before any is adopted (rule 8; stage 3 builds the game as a
  library with this compiler on the Mac, so the gate measures what the phone will run):
  - LLVM's SLP vectorizer on functions of huge blocks: one PPU unit takes 35 s with it, 3.3 s without; typical units
    17% less. Its code is no smaller with it.
  - The greedy register allocator's region growing on SPU functions that keep 90 vector registers live across
    thousands of blocks: a budget of 1,000 (`-grow-region-complexity-budget`, LLVM's default 10,000) makes the slowest
    program 2.3 times faster to compile and its code 30% smaller.
  - The SPU analyzer copies into each function the code of other functions it branches or falls into: block starts
    repeat 1.1-3.7 times in the 12 biggest programs.
  - Every PPU unit parses the game's whole prototype list (85,401 lines, 0.22 s): per-unit prototypes save 12%.
- **Memory:** a PPU unit peaks at +200 MB, a big SPU program at +500-900 MB, ten at once at 5.6 GB on the Mac. The
  phone's preparation schedules by predicted memory, not by core count (stage 4).
- **The user's ask for stage 4:** "Preparing game…" shows a loader with progress and an ETA that is accurate. Progress
  and ETA count predicted cost, not files (a few files take most of the time): each file's cost from its size and its
  largest functions, fitted on the Mac's per-file timings, scaled by the phone's own measured speed and corrected live
  as files finish, by simulating the remaining schedule over the workers.
- **Licence:** LLVM is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, whose exception lets it combine with GPLv2 code (D-001), as RPCS3
  does.
- **Not chosen now:** a direct ARM64 emitter (kept as the option if phone preparation times miss the budget after the
  fixes above), and emitting LLVM IR from the lifters instead of C (skips the front end: a later speed-up).

## D-152 · 2026-10-05 · A game's translated code is a library the host loads (route B, stage 3)

Route B (D-147) needs the translated code of a game to arrive after the app is built: a library the phone makes once
per game (D-150 signs it, D-151 compiles it) and the app loads. Stage 3 makes that library and loads it, on the Mac
first (rule 2).
- **The interface (runtime/game, `pspocket/game/library.h`):** a game library exports one symbol,
  `pspocket_game_library`. The host calls it with `ps_game_runtime`: pointers to the 18 PPU and 9 SPU runtime functions
  translated code calls, the PPU dispatch table and the four SPU reciprocal tables (the whole list, from the lifters'
  output and an `nm -u` of GTA V's code). The library returns `ps_game_library`: its register functions, its D-098
  image samples, the title, what made it, and the decrypted executable's SHA-256. Inside the library the runtime's
  names are hidden pointer variables (`PS_PPU_IMPORT` and `PS_SPU_IMPORT` in runtime.h, the tables in fp.h, under
  `PSPOCKET_GAME_LIBRARY`), filled in by the library's entry (`library/library_entry.c`, compiled into every library):
  the lifters' output does not change, and the host need not export anything, which a stripped iOS app could not.
- **Compatibility:** the build hashes the ten headers translated code includes and library.h (`ps_game_abi_hash`)
  and the lifters' sources (`ps_game_translator_hash`, cmake/GameAbiHash.cmake). A library carries both; the host
  binds only one with its own layout version and ABI hash, and only for the executable now in memory (its sampled
  words), else refuses with the reason and registers nothing; another translator hash is logged (a newer pspocket
  would translate the game differently).
- **Loading (`game::load_library`):** a fresh copy of the file (the kernel keeps a file's first signature), its
  signature registered and library validation asked (`codesign::register_signature`, as in D-150), dlopen, bind,
  checks, then its PPU functions and SPU programs registered. Never unloaded.
- **Building (runtime/codegen `build_library`, the phone's and the Mac's):** every file compiled by the device's
  compiler (D-151), the slowest first, as many at once as the cores and a memory budget allow; objects named by
  everything that makes them and kept, so a stopped build resumes (the first GTA V build failed at 681 of 815 files
  on a bug of ours and the next run compiled only the rest); then lld, and the library is signed. Progress and the
  time left count each file's predicted cost (`estimate_cost`: size, and lines times block starts per function for
  SPU code, fitted on run 092), corrected by the files done and laid out over the workers (`TimeLeft`): the user asked
  for an accurate time left.
- **pspocket-prepare** makes a game library on the Mac from ppu-lift's and lift-spu.sh's output, as the phone will;
  **`pspocket-boot --game-library FILE`** runs from one instead of the built-in translation; **`scripts/gate.sh game
  --library FILE`** walks the gate with it.
- **GTA V (run 093):** 815 files, 8 min 21 s on the M4's ten cores, linked in 1.2 s, 145 MB. The gate walk from the
  library passes with the built-in build's numbers: 29.8 fps median and 29.2 slowest, 2 frame jumps, 84 passes a
  frame, 1.6 GB; CPU within 3% (11.97 against 11.68 CPU-seconds per 5 s, run-to-run noise is of that size).
- **Test (tests/game):** recomp/ppu's synthetic benchmark, lifted at build time, made into a library with the
  device's compiler, loaded through the runtime table and run through the dispatch table: the natively computed
  result. A library made for another runtime, or for another executable, is refused and registers nothing; a second
  build compiles nothing; TimeLeft's arithmetic.
- **Kept:** the built-in path (`PSPOCKET_GAME_PPU/SPU`) stays until the app prepares games itself (stage 4).

## D-153 · 2026-10-05 · How translated code compiles, and how the time left is counted

- **Settings (`codegen::translated_code_settings`), for the Mac and the phone alike:** PPU code without LLVM's SLP
  vectorizer (`-fno-slp-vectorize`: one GTA V unit took 35 s with it and 3.3 s without, its code 44% smaller; the
  others 17% faster), and the greedy register allocator with a region-growing budget of 1,000 instead of 10,000
  (`-grow-region-complexity-budget`: the slowest SPU program compiles 2.3 times faster and its code is 30% smaller).
  GTA V compiles in 6:47 instead of 8:21 on the M4 (19%) and runs the gate the same: 29.8 fps, the CPU over the walk
  within the 12% the Mac varies between runs of one library (run 094). Measured, not assumed (rule 8): the gain at run
  time first seen was that noise.
- **The time left (`TimeLeft`, `estimate_cost`):** three kinds of file, each with its own rate (PPU code, SPU code, the
  registration tables, which compile in no time and were predicted as code); costs refitted on two builds with each
  build's own speed taken out; the prior rate weighs a quarter of the build's predicted cost, at most 1,000
  cost-seconds, because the first files to finish are the ones that ran fast (trusting them made the estimate 40% low
  a tenth of the way in). Replayed on both recorded builds, the time left is within 15% at every point, 5-8% on
  average. `pspocket-prepare --events` records a build's files so the next change to the estimate is tried the same way.
- Still to try, each against the gate: the SPU analyzer's copies of other functions' code, per-unit prototypes, clang
  built with PGO and LTO (docs/improve.md).

## D-154 · 2026-10-05 · Preparing a game on the phone: the pipeline, the screen, what is checked (route B, stage 4)

The phone makes a game's library itself, the first time the game is played: route B's promise (D-147), on top of
signing (D-150), compiling (D-151), libraries (D-152) and the compile settings and time left (D-153).
- **One pipeline for the Mac and the phone (runtime/prepare):** the executable's PPU functions translated
  (`recomp::ppu::translate_executable`, which ppu-lift --elf now shares: byte-identical output for GTA V; units of
  about 12,000 instructions), every file compiled (`codegen::build_library`), linked, signed (the user's identity on
  the phone, ad hoc on the Mac), then a manifest: the executable's SHA-256, the ABI and translator hashes, the
  compiler and the CPU it compiled for, the timings and the compile rate per kind of file. One progress and time left
  over all the steps (GTA V: translating takes 6 s of the 7.5 minutes). The translated C (0.8 GB for GTA V) is deleted
  once the library is made; the objects stay, so a stopped preparation goes on from where it was.
- **When a game is prepared again:** no library; another ABI hash (another pspocket); another executable (an update);
  another CPU (a backup restored to another phone: the phone compiles for its own chip, `-mcpu` from LLVM's host
  detection, which takes chips newer than it knows, the A19 Pro included, as its newest, apple-m4). Another translator
  hash leaves the library in use (a newer pspocket would translate the game differently; preparing it again is for
  later).
- **The screen:** Play on a game without a library shows "Preparing <game> for this iPhone": a bar that fills by time,
  the step ("Compiling: 312 of 811 files"), and the time left, followed with a time constant of about six seconds and
  said the way a person says it ("About 7 minutes left", "Less than a minute left"). The screen stays on. Cancel stops
  at the next file and keeps what is compiled. The next game's time left starts from the speeds this phone measured
  last time (`last-preparation/manifest.json`).
- **When it cannot:** no signing identity on the phone yet, no compiler in the build, or a failure: the game starts
  the way it did before route B (the translation built into the app if it is this game's, else the interpreters), and
  the library shows why.
- **SPU programs:** a library made on the phone has none yet; the app's built-in ones (found by their code's hash, so
  never for another game) run with it. Next (stage 4c): the phone lifts the SPU programs too, from images found in
  the executable (264 of GTA V's 265 are in EBOOT.elf as they are) and those the game loads at run time.
- **On the Mac:** `pspocket-prepare --title ID --exe EBOOT.elf --game-dir DIR [--spu DIR]` runs the same pipeline;
  GTA V prepared from its executable alone (and the Mac's lifted SPU programs) passes the gate (run 095).

## D-155 · 2026-10-06 · The phone translates a game's SPU programs too, finding code only registers reach

Stage 4c of route B. The Mac lifted GTA V's SPU programs with scripts/lift-spu.sh from the images its runs saved, and
the seeds those runs accumulated (D-099): the phone has neither the script nor the runs.
- **`lift_spu_images` (runtime/prepare/spu.cpp)** is lift-spu.sh in C++: the saved images (spu_<hash>_<ls>.bin and
  .txt), seeds from their "seed" lines, from runs' miss logs and from every entry of an earlier lift in the same
  folder, relocatable copies merged once per hash at the first copy's base, one directory per program and
  game_spu.c. For GTA V's 265 images it writes byte for byte what the script writes (150 programs, in under a second).
  The phone uses the images the app already saves while a game runs (pspocket-coverage/<title>/spu, D-117) and its
  miss log; a game that met SPU programs since its library was made is updated (only those compile).
- **Discovery (`AnalyzerOptions::discover`, on in the pipeline):** translated from the images alone, GTA V's programs
  missed 379 entries the Mac runs had taught the script, and the walk ran at 12.8 fps. The misses were code reached only
  through registers: after an unconditional branch (182, jump table cases), after calls in functions only pointers
  reach (148), after returns and stops. The analyzer now also starts from every instruction after one that never falls
  through, padding skipped, that nothing reached, and stops where it meets code already reached (entered there, a
  label of the function holding it, rather than copied: 112 MB of C without that rule, 92 MB with it, the Mac-seeded set
  86 MB). 353 of the 379 are found.
- **Discovered code does not make a program stale:** a program is dropped when a DMA writes over one of its translated
  instructions (D-085); discovery also translates data that decodes as code, which the jobs write, so whole jobs were
  dropped and interpreted (12 fps). The lifter leaves discovered functions out of a program's code words. With that,
  GTA V from SPU code translated from its images alone runs the gate walk at 29.8 fps (45 misses left, logged: the next
  update adds them; run 096). The risk taken: real code only discovery found and an overlay overwrites would run stale.
- **The app's built-in SPU programs first:** programs are found by hash, the first registered winning, so the app
  registers the ones built into it before a library's (their entries come from the Mac's runs); a library fills in
  what the app lacks. `pspocket-boot --builtin-spu` and `gate.sh --builtin-spu` do the same; without it a library
  runs alone, to test what it holds.

## D-156 · 2026-10-06 · /dev_flash from the user's PS3UPDAT.PUP, on the phone

Stage 5's first half: no Mac for the system software either. recomp/common reads a PUP (RPCS3 Loader/PUP.h: the
"SCEUF" header and file table; the entries' HMACs are not checked) and ustar archives (Loader/TAR.cpp), and decrypts an
SCE package as RPCS3's SCEDecrypter does (unself.cpp: the metadata info opened with the package key, the sections
with their own keys, zlib inflated). `install_firmware` takes the update archive (file 0x300), every dev_flash_*
package in it, and writes each package's third section (a TAR) under /dev_flash, as RPCS3's firmware installer does.
The package key (key_vault.h SCEPKG_ERK/RIV) comes into the build directory with the SELF keys (scripts/self-keys.py),
never into the repository. On the M4: 4.92's 24 packages, 1,075 files, 186 MB in 1.4 s, and all 142 modules of
sys/external then decrypt with pspocket's own SELF code (run 096). The app installs it from Settings › System
software into Application Support/pspocket-firmware/dev_flash, which games then mount. The second half, loading
firmware modules (LLE) where pspocket has no HLE, is next.

## D-157 · 2026-10-06 · Firmware modules run as they are where pspocket has nothing (LLE, route B stage 5)

Any game may import a library pspocket never implemented; with the user's system software installed (D-156), the PS3's
own module serves it instead of every call failing. runtime/loader/lle.cpp does what RPCS3's ppu_load_prx,
ppu_load_exports and ppu_load_imports do (PPUModule.cpp): the module (a SELF in /dev_flash/sys/external) decrypted with
pspocket's SELF code, its LOAD segments placed in main memory, its SCE_PPURELA relocations applied (types 1, 4, 5, 6,
10, 11, 38, 44, 57; a bad entry is logged and skipped), its exports read (the management library's module_start and
module_stop, every library's functions and variables), its own imports linked to the host's stubs or to other firmware
modules, recursively. The game's import slots get the module's descriptors and its variable references the module's
addresses; the main thread runs each module_start (dependencies first, r3 = r4 = 0) after sys_initialize_tls and
before the entry, as ppu_load_exec does. Firmware code runs under the interpreter (the dispatch miss policy is
already "interpret").

The policy is per module file, not per function: a module goes LLE only when the host implements none of the libraries
it exports. Mixing host and firmware functions of one library would split its state (SPURS, sysutil, the GCM context),
and RPCS3 also chooses per library. So the libraries pspocket runs on the host (lv2, SPURS (D-037), the RSX, files,
sysutil, network, NP) are never doubled, and a library a host function exists for keeps its gaps as logged errors
(rule 4). `--lle LIBRARY` (pspocket-boot) forces one onto its module to test it; `--no-lle` turns modules off. The
index of which file exports which library is built once per firmware (all 142 modules of 4.92 decrypt; 163 libraries;
2.5 s on the M4) and kept in lle-index.txt beside /dev_flash. pspocket-boot uses modules whenever --flash is given,
the app whenever the system software is installed.

First real run (run 097): Assassin's Creed with `--lle cellSync`, which libsre.sprx exports beside cellSpurs: the
firmware's cellSync replaces the main thread's 24-million-call spin on the missing cellSyncMutexTryLock, and the game
goes on to its next gaps (sys_mmapper_allocate_memory). Its own libraries all have host functions, so by default it
loads no module. A module's imported variables come from the module that exports them (its reference tables patched,
as ppu_patch_refs; with attribute 0x2000 a function's reference table too): libadec links 17 of its codecs' variables,
and the 17 modules of `--lle-load cellAdec --lle-load cellDmux` all ran their module_start to 0 under the interpreter
(run 097). Not yet: modules a game loads itself through sys_prx (syscalls 480-499), and translating firmware code
with the game.

## D-158 · 2026-10-06 · New shaders compile in the background: a frame waits for them 4 ms at most

Rendering any game, not one: route B runs games the phone has never seen, and nothing records their shaders on a Mac
first (the Mac's recording comes with the app for GTA V only, D-118). Until now each program and pipeline new to the
backend compiled on the RSX thread at the draw that first needed it. GTA V with an empty shader cache on the M4 (run
098): 562 programs and pipelines in one 300-frame stretch of the first walk, 9.3 s of stalls, 5 s windows at 6.8 and
14.2 fps, 12.7 s of stalls in 128 s; the iPhone compiles several times slower.
- `AsyncCompiler` (runtime/rsx/metal/src/async_compiler.mm): a program or pipeline a draw lacks is queued (a program
  translated to MSL on the RSX thread, as before, compiled with newLibraryWithSource on a worker; a pipeline once its
  two programs exist, its descriptor built on the RSX thread) on half the cores (2 to 4), at user-initiated QoS.
  Pipelines go first: each is the last thing its draw waits for.
- The RSX thread waits for what its draw queued while the frame's budget lasts (`compile_wait_ms`, 4 ms, renewed at
  each flip), taking whatever finishes meanwhile; past it the draw is skipped ("compiling", counted per frame in the
  report and the run summary), as RPCS3's asynchronous shader mode skips draws. What finishes joins the caches
  between draws and is recorded in the shader cache, so the next launch makes it ahead (D-114).
- A compile that fails is logged once and not tried again.
- The app turns it on; pspocket-boot with `--async-shaders MS`. The gate keeps waiting compiles: its frames are
  compared, and its shader cache has everything anyway.

Measured (run 098, same walk, empty cache, a Mac busy with other builds): the slowest 5 s windows 25.0 and 27.2 fps
(late in the walk, where little compiled) instead of 6.8 and 14.2; the RSX thread spent 0.5 s instead of 9.3 s in the
burst. The price is draws left out while their shaders compile: 117 per frame on average over the burst's 300
frames (287 with programs first and two threads). Tests: a draw with no budget goes without its programs and draws once they
are made, with nothing compiled on the RSX thread; with a budget that covers the compiles it waits and draws.

## D-159 · 2026-10-06 · Modules a game loads while it runs (sys_prx)

Many games keep part of their code in PRX modules on the disc and load them with sys_prx_load_module; route B's "any
ISO" needs that. sysPrxForUser gets sys_prx_load_module, sys_prx_load_module_list, sys_prx_start_module,
sys_prx_stop_module, sys_prx_unload_module and sys_prx_get_module_id_by_name, as RPCS3's wrappers (sys_prx_.cpp): the
start and stop functions run on the calling thread (call_guest), args and argp passed, their result written to the
caller's result and given back (SYS_PRX_RESIDENT keeps the module; anything else unloads it, as _sys_prx_start_module
cmd 2). A recursive host mutex stands for liblv2's "_lv2prx" lwmutex. The placing and linking is the loader's,
behind hle::ModuleLoader: RuntimeModules reads the file through the game's own file system (Kernel::vfs_read_file:
the disc image, /app_home, /dev_hdd0), decrypts a disc game's SELF with the built-in keys (an NPDRM module needs the
game's klicensee: refused, CELL_PRX_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_PRX_TYPE), and places and links it as D-157 does a firmware
module, its imports going to modules loaded before it, then firmware modules, then the host. Starting a module
points the executable's import slots (and reference tables, and imported variables) of its libraries at its exports,
as lv2_prx::load_exports; until then they hold the host's stubs. A path in /dev_flash/sys/external goes to the
firmware module when the host replaces none of its libraries, else an empty module whose libraries the host serves
(RPCS3's "ignored" modules). Unloading keeps the memory (code of it may still be on a stack). The HLE stub tables
are sized for 65,536 functions up front, so linking while guest threads call stubs never moves what they read.
Not yet: fixed-address loading (flags 1, CELL_ENOSYS), sys_prx_get_module_list/info, and translating a game's
modules in the preparation (they run interpreted). Test: a game's module loaded from /app_home, its module_start run,
the game's import repointed, the state errors (started twice, unloaded while started), name lookup.

## D-160 · 2026-10-06 · Assassin's Creed's 40 missing functions, as RPCS3 has them, with what differs

Three agents implemented the 40 imports Assassin's Creed (BLES00158) used and pspocket lacked, each from RPCS3 and,
for SPURS and cellSync, checked against the firmware's libsre as a reference only (D-046); 21 test cases, every guest
store that other processors may race through the reservation system. Where pspocket differs from RPCS3, and why:
- **cellSyncMutex** Initialize/TryLock/Unlock: a ticket lock in one word; TryLock writes nothing when busy (a game
  polling it must not break other code's reservations on the line), and every write is a reservation_op: a plain host
  compare-and-swap, as RPCS3 uses, let a guest conditional store merge around it (two holders, caught by the test).
- **cellMsgDialogOpen2**: answered at the first cellSysutilCheckCallback (OK, or YES/NO by the default cursor), as
  the keyboard dialog (D-140); RPCS3 without its UI never answers. Dialogs without buttons stay until Abort.
- **cellFsAio** Init/Read/Cancel/Finish: RPCS3's live code never starts the AIO thread ("use LLE"); pspocket runs its
  unused fs_aio_thread design on a real lv2 thread (internal function, priority 1000, 64 KB stack): reads at the
  request's offset without moving the file position, then the callback. Cancel stays CELL_EINVAL (a TODO in RPCS3).
- **cellFsGetFreeSize**: RPCS3's three disk-free syscalls' rules done in sys_fs (40 GB less 256 KB on /dev_hdd0).
- **cellHddGameCheck, cellGameDataCheckCreate2, cellDiscGameGetBootDiscInfo,
  cellDiscGameRegisterDiscChangeCallback** (kept; the disc never changes), **cellAudioOutSetCopyControl**: RPCS3's
  structures and checks; error dialogs logged, its sleeps skipped (D-044); a PARAM.SFO the host cannot write is
  CELL_GAMEDATA_ERROR_ACCESS_ERROR where RPCS3 aborts.
- **cellPad** ClearBuf, GetInfo (648-byte layout, max_connect not clamped, vendor/product 054C:0268),
  GetCapabilityInfo.
- **cellGcmSys** SetFlipMode (through lv2's display-sync attribute; before cellGcmInit only logged), GetTimeStamp,
  GetReport, GetReportDataAddress, SetTile (lv2's refusal of an odd tile is returned), SetFlip (RPCS3's "put + 8"
  kept exactly), SetWaitFlip.
- **cellSpurs** CreateTaskset, _cellSpursSendSignal, AddUrgentCommand (four slots, then JOB_ERROR_BUSY).
- **sysPrxForUser** spinlocks (0xABADCAFE, polite waiting through lv2's yield), the mmapper wrappers,
  sys_process_is_stack, sys_spu_image_close (kernel images: syscall 158 is missing, CELL_ENOSYS),
  sys_game_process_exitspawn (the parameter block built byte for byte; the next executable is not launched).
- Pointers outside guest memory are refused with the call site logged (D-042), where RPCS3 would fault.

With them the game boots on the Mac to its autosave notice and its disclaimer, at 60 fps (run 099).
