## D-202 · 2026-10-06 · cellGifDec is pspocket's own, the same as Sony's libgifdec

The last of step 3's image decoders: cellGifDec's seven functions are pspocket's (runtime/hle/src/cellGifDec.cpp), with
its own LZW decoder. Sony's libgifdec is giflib (its allocations show giflib's 12-byte colour maps and the 0x6148-byte
private state holding the LZW tables) behind Sony's API; what it does was measured call by call (run 108):

- **Records.** Each DecodeData returns the file's next record: an extension (label, and a pointer to its sub-blocks
  with their terminator, in a buffer libgifdec took at Open and grows a sub-block at a time in whole 0x100s), an
  image, or the trailer. Once the parameters are set the status is written first (0); a stop asked through
  commandPtr writes 1 and decodes nothing.
- **Images.** An image record is the whole logical screen, 4 bytes a pixel (RGBA or ARGB): every pixel the background
  index looked up in the image's own colour table (the local one if it has one), the image at its place (interlaced
  rows put back in order); a pixel whose index, the background's included, is the transparent one of the last graphic
  control extension gets alpha1 with its colour kept, every other alpha2. The transparency stays for later images
  until another graphic control extension. No earlier image shows through. The game's row padding is not touched.
- **LZW.** giflib's decoding (dgif_lib.c): codes from the low bit, the width growing with the table up to 12 bits and
  kept there, a code past the next free one a defect; the rest of the data skipped to its terminator.
- **Errors.** An image past the screen, no colour table, a defect, cut data, no trailer: STREAM_FORMAT, the game's
  buffer untouched. A cut colour table or a file not starting "GIF": STREAM_FORMAT from ReadHeader (the version is not
  checked). A call out of order answers SEQ and fails the stream for everything but Close; a row pitch narrower than
  the image ARG; reading past the trailer SEQ.
- **Numbers.** Codec version 0x240000; initSpaceAllocated 0x6D70; useMemorySpace width x height + 4 x height + 40.
- **Memory.** pspocket takes from the game's allocator what libgifdec takes, in the same order (Create 0x380, plus
  0x33880 with SPU threads; Open 0x140, 0x100, 0x5C, 0x6148; colour tables; each image's raster and row pointers),
  and gives it all back at Close and Destroy, so the extension pointer and the game's memory are the same.
- **Not reproduced:** the bytes in libgifdec's extension buffer past an extension's terminator (its own state), and a
  background index past the colour table (libgifdec reads past its table; pspocket gives black). Not pspocket's yet:
  the Ext functions (a game importing one gets Sony's whole libgifdec, D-175).

Measured: 1131 answers and 85 images, the same with SPU threads off and on (18 GIFs built in code by
tests/hle/gif_writer.hpp: 87a and 89a, global and local tables of 2 to 256 colours, frames inside and past the screen,
interlacing down to one row, code sizes 2 to 8, early clear codes, short sub-blocks, a full table with and without a
clear, every extension kind, animations; six damaged files; eight call orders; stop and continue).

## D-203 · 2026-10-07 · Jump tables: a bounds check that branches into the table code, and tail calls as a way out

Assassin's Creed's switch at 0xa88f18 jumped through the interpreter 86 times a session ("indirect jump to 0x00a88fb4
has no lifted function"). Its table address is in the game's data, two loads away (r30 from the TOC in the prologue,
then the table's address from r30's block), and the analyzer reads it on its second pass with the prologue's
constants (D-096). Two things threw that pass away:

- **Tail calls.** The prefix constants hold only if nothing else in the function writes the register, apart from the
  restores on the way out. Each case of this switch restores r30 and then branches to another function (GCC's tail
  call), and only a restore running into `blr` counted as the way out. Now an unconditional branch out of the
  function counts too; a restore followed by a branch back into the function still does not.
- **The bounds check.** GCC put the table code at the branch target: `cmplwi cr7, r0, 4; ble cr7, table_code`, the
  default case falling through to the epilogue. The matcher looked for the check only on the straight-line path into
  the table code. When that code starts right after an unconditional exit, the one branch into it is now taken as the
  guard (`ble`: max + 1 entries, `blt`: max), and the index must stay unchanged from the compare to the branch and
  from the block's start to the table load. A second way into the block leaves the table unbounded, as before.

Measured on the executables' translation: Assassin's Creed 599 to 620 tables, 144 to 64 analyzer warnings (80 tables
bounded that were scanned before); GTA V 133 tables either way, 126 to 124 warnings. A guess made first (the words
after the bctr taken as the table when the base cannot be read) was dropped: the base can be read, so it was not the
cause, and nothing else needs it.

## D-204 · 2026-10-07 · An SPU module cut by a later copy keeps its identity while its code is intact

The module tracker (D-079) knows a module by the run of GETs that copied it into local store. A later GET over part of
a run used to drop the whole run, so a module whose tail a task then filled with data ran interpreted (Assassin's
Creed: a 42 KB module at 0x4c00, data over its last 10 KB, run 109).

- **What stays.** A run cut by a copy keeps the extent it was copied with (its identity: hash, size, where it was
  lifted) and the part still in local store (where it holds code): the part before the copy, else the part after it.
  One the copy covers entirely is gone. Only the part still there must equal its guest copy.
- **Only data may be written over.** The cut part must not hold any word the program lifted as an instruction (its
  code words, D-085): a branch there would run the old code where the copy now is. Then the module runs
  interpreted, as before. A run cut after it was identified is identified again when it runs next.
- The first half (the identity kept) went in with ffe091c by mistake, under a docs message; acaddd9 adds the code
  check. Test: tests/hle/test_spu_programs.cpp, a module with data over its tail, its code, its head, and all of it.

## D-205 · 2026-10-07 · SPU code only a constant reaches is speculative; prepare carries over the seeds it used

Assassin's Creed's busiest job chain (workload 1) ran interpreted: 64.8 billion SPU instructions at LS 0x4c00 in a
six-minute session (run 114), 11.2 billion in 200 s (run 115). Each job writes into its own binary's tail (a 4-byte
DMA at +0xa730, its own data), and the translated program claimed those words as instructions, so the DMA dropped the
program (D-085) and the cached binary ran interpreted from then on. The words were the job's shuffle patterns and the
zeros after them (`stop 0` falls through, so tracing ran on to the image's end). The cause, and the same hole
where constants start functions:

- **Prepare promoted guesses to code.** Each prepare took every entry of the previous program as a seed, and a
  program's entries are all its labels, also those of code only discovery (D-155) found. As seeds they counted as
  code on the next prepare. Now each program directory keeps NAME.seeds, the seeds that lift used (the images' seed
  lines and the runs' logs), and the next prepare carries over those. An output from before has no such file and
  contributes nothing. Test: tests/game/test_prepare_spu.cpp (a job prepared twice keeps its code words).
- **Code a constant points at.** An ila/il constant that points into the image starts a function when constants are
  entries (the default outside jobs and modules: thread images, the firmware's programs). Such a function is now
  speculative unless an entry, a seed or a direct call from code that is reaches it, and like discovered code it is
  lifted and entered but left out of the code words. A DMA over it does not make the program stale; a program that
  overwrote such a function with other code would run the old one (as with discovered code since D-155). Test:
  tests/spu/test_discover.cpp.

The job's code words went from 10,656 to 4,389 of its 10,764 words.

## D-206 · 2026-10-07 · An SPU module whose guest copy changed is known by its local store copy

The module tracker identified a module by hashing its guest copy, and refused one whose local store copy no longer
matched it ("changed before it ran"), in case the module had been patched where it runs. Assassin's Creed copies a
32 KB module to LS 0x33980 and then reuses the guest buffer before the module runs (all 6,705 words differ, in every
run): local store holds the module intact, and it ran interpreted.

- A module still whole in local store (no later copy cut it, D-204) whose guest copy differs is identified by the
  bytes in local store: they are the code that runs, so a program lifted from them is right whichever copy changed.
  A module patched where it runs gets no program by that hash (unless such a patched copy was saved and lifted
  before) and is interpreted, as before; with --spu-dump the local store copy is what gets saved.
- A module cut by a later copy and changed in the part still there stays interpreted (its identity is the whole
  copy, which local store no longer holds).

Test: tests/hle/test_spu_programs.cpp (a module whose guest buffer is reused before it runs).

## D-207 · 2026-10-07 · The PPU interpreter's share is counted and reported, as the SPU's is

The runs reported how much SPU code ran interpreted, per site, but not PPU code: the fallbacks (an indirect call or
jump with no translated function) and Assassin's Creed's fiber switches (D-161, whose loops never return to translated
code) were visible only as one log line each. The goal is no interpreting, so it must be measured.

- The interpreter counts instructions per address it was entered at (ps_ppu_interp_sites: a lock-free table of 4,096
  sites, the SPU's layout). A run adds its count every 65,536 instructions as well as at its end, so a loop that never
  returns shows while it runs. One masked compare per interpreted instruction.
- pspocket-boot logs "PPU interpreted: N instructions in 5.0 s" beside the frame rate when there were any, and the
  twelve busiest sites at the end ("PPU interpreted: N instructions from M entries at 0x...").

Test: tests/ppu/test_interp_branch_mem.cpp (a loop's count and entries, a run stopped by its step limit).

## D-208 · 2026-10-07 · An SPU program is also known by its code words alone

A task of Assassin's Creed loads one 32 KB module into its own data area at LS 0x33980 and calls 0x37c58, about twice
a second. Its whole-image hash was new every time: 398 different images in run 117, so it ran interpreted (81 million
instructions a session). The 56 copies run 118 saved differ only in 18 words at the module's end, a parameter block;
the other 8,078 words are the same. Whole-image hashing cannot name such a module, however many copies are lifted.

- **Code hash.** Each lifted SPU program carries `code_hash`: ps_spu_hash64 over the bytes of its code words only
  (the words it lifted as instructions, D-085, D-155, D-205). Programs lifted before the field leave it zero (not
  known); generated code may omit trailing fields (-Wno-missing-field-initializers for generated sources).
- **At run time.** A relocatable image (job or module) whose whole hash no program has is checked against the
  relocatable programs of its size: one whose code words hold the same bytes is the program. The data is read from
  local store at run time, as with any program, so it may be anything. Cost: one hash over the code words of each
  candidate, only for images not found by their whole hash.
- **In prepare.** A relocatable image whose code words match a program lifted earlier in the same preparation is
  merged into it instead of lifted again (the 57 saved copies of that module give one program).
- What it does not cover: code that itself changes with the load (patched instructions) stays a different program,
  as it must.

Tests: tests/hle/test_spu_programs.cpp (a module loaded with other data three times stays lifted; other code does
not), tests/game/test_prepare_spu.cpp (copies differing in data are lifted once).

## D-209 · 2026-10-07 · "Time left" knows the kept files before the first compile

Preparing a game again keeps every object whose source and settings are unchanged. The time left shown until the
first file finished still counted every file: Assassin's Creed prepared again with 404 of 410 files kept said 3:18 for
a 0:16 job. The first estimate comes from the executable's size, before translation, and the compile phase only
reported when files started or finished. The build now reports once as soon as it knows which files it keeps, before
the first compile, with the time left of the files it will compile (none kept: the same model as before; all kept:
0). The estimate before translation stays a guess from the executable's size.

Test: tests/game/test_game_library.cpp (the first report comes before any file, and says 0 when every file is kept).

## D-210 · 2026-10-07 · Shader programs uploaded again are found by their words, not decoded again

In Assassin's Creed's crowd (the training's "Gentle Push", run 121: 2,150 draws a frame) the RSX thread was the busiest
thread, 81% of a core, about 13 µs per draw. A profile (macOS `sample`, 15 s, run 122) put 7% of it in decoding vertex
programs and 3.7% in decoding fragment programs: the game uploads its vertex program again before nearly every draw,
and writes its fragment programs' embedded constants in place, and each time the backend decoded the whole program
again only to find the compile it already had.

- **Vertex programs.** The backend keeps the 16 programs it decoded last, each with its words from its start to its
  end (what the decoder read: the result depends on nothing else). After an upload it compares the words at the
  start slot with each (memcmp) and takes the one that matches, compiled lookups included; only a new program is
  decoded.
- **Fragment programs.** After a write to a program's memory, its bytes are compared with the ones it was decoded
  from, embedded constants left out (they are read every draw anyway): the same instructions keep the decode and its
  compiles, and only the watch is set again.
- Measured on the crowd (run 122 against run 123, the same walk, windows without the sampler): 25 to 28.8 fps to 29
  to 30.2 (the game's 30 cap there); the RSX thread 3.9-4.1 s to 3.4-3.8 s of CPU per 5 s, about 13.0 to 11.6-12.2 µs
  per draw. The decoders left the profile; copying (vertex data and constants, 19%) is the next cost.

Tests: tests/rsx/test_metal.mm (two vertex programs alternating at one start and a third differing in one word; a
fragment program with new constants, new instructions, then its first form again).

## D-211 · 2026-10-07 · Vertex data copied once per buffer; fragment programs checked by their bytes, unprotected

Two more costs of the RSX thread in Assassin's Creed's crowd (D-210's profile and the per-frame numbers):

- **Interleaved vertices copied several times.** Each enabled attribute copied its own range of guest memory into the
  draw's upload; with interleaved vertices (position, normal, texture coordinates side by side) those ranges overlap
  almost entirely, so a mesh with six attributes was copied about six times per draw. Now the ranges are merged
  (overlapping or touching ones), each group is copied once, and its attributes point into that copy at their offset
  (the shader reads bytes at any offset). The backend counts the bytes it copies (BackendStats::vertex_bytes_copied).
- **Write faults on fragment programs.** A fragment program's memory was write-protected to notice changes; the game
  writes the program's embedded constants in place before each draw, so each draw cost the game's thread a write
  fault and the RSX thread an mprotect to protect it again: 170 to 210 faults a frame. Since D-210 the backend compares
  the program's bytes with the ones it decoded (constants left out) anyway, so fragment programs are no longer
  protected: the same check runs at the same moments (the program set again, or a new batch of commands).
- Measured on the crowd: the copying in the draw from about 11% of the RSX thread to 3.6% (run 124); write faults 170
  to 210 a frame to 0.1 (run 125); the RSX thread 3.2-3.5 s to 3.0-3.4 s per 5 s, about 11.1 to 11.6 µs per draw
  (13.0 before D-210); 30.4 to 31.8 fps.

Tests: tests/rsx/test_metal.mm (interleaved position and colour drawn right, 60 bytes copied, not 100; D-210's
fragment program test covers the check).

## D-213 · 2026-10-07 · A non-local jump goes back to run_guest by _longjmp, not a C++ exception

D-161 made a longjmp or a fiber switch in translated code throw lv2::NonLocalJump from the lifter's marker syscall to
run_guest, which goes on in the interpreter. Assassin's Creed switches fibers about 12,000 times a second in its later
scenes (run 128: 8.1 million in 690 s, through the interpreter at its setjmp's return, 0xcf6d90), and a profile of
its two task threads in the crowd (run 127) showed most of their time in the C++ unwinder: dyld looking up the image
of every frame, and the unwinder's lock (the two threads contend for it). One of them was 76% busy, mostly unwinding.

- run_guest keeps a per-thread stack of targets (its own jmp_buf, the outer one restored when it returns or an
  exception leaves it) and Kernel::syscall jumps to the innermost with _longjmp as its first act on the marker.
  _setjmp/_longjmp, not setjmp: on Darwin setjmp saves the signal mask with a system call.
- Why it is safe: between that point and run_guest there are only translated C frames and the interpreter's
  (trivially destructible locals) and the syscall entry before it constructs anything. Every way from host code into
  guest code (a thread's entry, call_guest's callbacks) goes through run_guest, so an HLE function's frame, which may
  hold objects with destructors, is always below the innermost target, never skipped. NonLocalJump stays for a thread
  with no run_guest (not expected).
- ThreadExit (process exit) is still an exception: rare, and it must run destructors.

Measured in the crowd (run 129 against runs 125 and 127, the same walk and windows): the two task threads from 5.45 to
1.89 s of CPU per 5 s, the whole process from 27.4-28.3 to 20.8 s per 5 s (a quarter less), 30-31 to 33.7 fps.

Test: tests/lv2/test_threads.cpp (an executor standing in for translated code makes the marker syscall with LR and r1
moved, three threads in a row: each goes on in the interpreter at the landing code and exits with its result; the
executor never gets control back).

## D-214 · 2026-10-07 · A texture decoded from memory gets every GPU-newer target it overlaps; one covered whole copies nothing

The RSX thread's profile in Assassin's Creed's crowd (run 129) still had about 15% in texture decoding: copying the
texture's bytes from guest memory (memmove), and watching and unwatching its pages (mprotect). New counts in the
per-frame line showed only 2 decodes a frame, both over a target drawn to again, and a one-off log of their shapes
showed why they were expensive, and also wrong:

- a 4096x1024 texture over a 1024x1024 depth buffer with a 16 KB row pitch: four depth buffers side by side (by the
  look of it the shadow cascades), sampled as one texture; and a 2560x720 texture over two 1280x720 depth buffers.
- D-137 laid over the decode only the target at the texture's own address. The others' part came from guest memory,
  which the GPU's drawing never reaches (targets are written back only when the RSX itself reads them): stale.

Now:
- **Every target in its rows.** A linear texture decoded from memory gets every GPU-newer target with its row pitch
  that its bytes overlap laid over the copy, oldest first after the one at its address (each synced with its
  children, D-122); a target that cannot be laid over is written back first. Targets with another layout inside the
  texture's range are left alone, as before (run 132 showed a compressed texture inside a big depth buffer's memory:
  memory the game may reuse). The cache entry keeps the list (serials and generations): any of them drawn to again,
  or a different set, decodes it again. As RPCS3 gathers the sections of a texture from its render targets.
- **Nothing copied when covered.** When the targets together write every texel position the decode reads (one linear
  level; each target with the texture's row pitch and all its rows; their columns together the texture's row),
  nothing is copied from memory and no watch is set: the texture holds while the overlays do (a CPU write there makes
  a target older than memory, and then it is not laid over).
- The backend counts textures decoded again over a target drawn to since or over written memory, the bytes copied for
  textures, and the textures that came from targets alone; a texture not covered logs its shape once.

Measured on the crowd (runs 129, 131, 132; the same walk and windows): the RSX thread 11.0 to 9.2 µs per draw, the
watching and unwatching gone from its profile. The gate passes (GTA V 29.8 fps, no new messages).

Tests: tests/rsx/test_metal.mm (two depth buffers side by side sampled as one texture show both, from the GPU, nothing
copied: with only the first laid over, the right half shows memory; a depth buffer sampled at its row size twice, from
the buffer each time; a texture with half a target's pitch inside its memory is not laid over); D-137's tests keep the
partial case (a texture larger than its target).

## D-215 · 2026-10-07 · cflts and cfltu in NEON

A profile of GTA V's prologue walk (run 134, macOS `sample`, 15 s) put 35% of the five main SPU threads' busy time in
one geometry job (spu_dad457863220b1cc), and its hottest lines in float-to-integer conversions (`cflts $r, $a, 173`)
between shuffles. The lifted code converted each lane through double precision in scalar code.

- When the scale 2^(173 - I8) is a normal float (I8 from 47 to 255, 173 the common plain conversion), the lanes are
  multiplied by it (exact, or past the integer range) and converted with FCVTZS/FCVTZU, which truncate and saturate as
  the SPU does. The SPU's float range is applied around it: exponent 0 is zero, exponent 255 (infinity or NaN to the
  host) is a huge number saturated by its sign. Other scales keep the scalar form.
- Checked: the differential fuzz test (every lifted instruction against the interpreter, 256 encodings of each, three
  more seeds of 200 contexts), and spu-check (D-132) on the 53 of GTA V's 300 programs that use cflts or cfltu: 2,679
  trials of the game's own translated functions against the interpreter, no difference. GTA V's walk: the main SPU
  threads 7.93 to 7.62 s of CPU per 5 s (4%, the same windows); the gate passes.
- History: D-127 had the same form, withdrawn with the rest of D-127 in D-131 when the EDGE/GFX chain stopped on the
  iPhone; D-138 later saw the same stops without D-127 (something writes over the chain's descriptors).

## D-216 · 2026-10-07 · D-127's call saves again: a call stores and reloads only what the callee can touch

Run 134's profile of GTA V: calls (brsl) were 13.5% of the SPU samples and the lines with no instruction (function
entry loads, exit stores) 22%. Each direct call stored every register the caller writes and reloaded every one it
uses, up to 127 of each. D-127 had made a call store only what the caller wrote of what the callee (and its callees)
may touch, and reload only what it uses of what they may write, with each caller storing the rest when the callee
leaves for the run loop; D-131 withdrew it with D-127's other changes when the EDGE/GFX chain stopped on the iPhone,
"until a check of the game's own translated functions against the interpreter finds what differs". D-138 saw the
same stops later without D-127 (something writes over the chain's descriptors), and that check now exists (D-132).

- The same rules, ported to today's lifter: a function's summary is what it and its callees use and write, to a fixed
  point; a stop or a call through a register (bisl) makes it everything. Other ways out (an absolute call in
  relocatable code, an indirect jump that is not the function's own label) leave for the run loop and store
  everything, as before. Reviewed again: the callee's entry loads come from ctx, which holds every register the
  caller wrote that the callee may read; the caller's other registers stay in its locals until it calls again or
  leaves; a callee that leaves has each caller up the chain store the rest.
- Checked: the program-level fuzz test of D-127 (registers kept across a call that does not touch them, read and
  written by the callee, written two calls deep, across a call that leaves for the run loop and comes back), and
  spu-check over all 150 of GTA V's programs (5,002 trials of its own functions against the interpreter, no
  difference). The gate passes.
- Measured (run 136, GTA V's walk, 60-90 s): the main SPU threads 7.62 to 7.33 s of CPU per 5 s, the audio SPU 1.88
  to 1.73, the process 13.0 to 12.4. What is left: each function's own loads at entry and stores at exit.

## D-217 · 2026-10-07 · Byte shifts and rotates in NEON, again

The third part of D-127 that D-131 withdrew: shlqby, rotqby and rotqmby (and their immediate and bit-count forms,
which use the same helpers) moved the 128-bit value through general registers (about 6 instructions for a constant
count, 30 and a branch for a register count). rotqby alone was 5.3% of GTA V's SPU samples (run 134). On AArch64 each
is one table lookup over the byte indices: host byte k of the result is byte k - n (left) or k + n (right) of the
operand, an index past 15 reading zero; the register layout is D-004's full reverse, so a guest shift left is a host
index shift down.

- Checked: the differential fuzz test (three seeds of 100 contexts, every encoding), spu-check over all 150 of GTA V's
  programs (5,002 trials, no difference), the gate.
- Measured (run 137, GTA V's walk, 60-90 s): the main SPU threads 7.33 to 6.98 s of CPU per 5 s, the audio SPU 1.73
  to 1.57, the process 12.4 to 11.9. Since run 134 (D-215 to D-217): the main SPU threads 12% less, the audio SPU 15%
  less, the process 11% less.

## D-218 · 2026-10-07 · shufb's special control bytes in one table lookup

The lifted shufb picked each byte with a two-register table lookup, then made the three special control values
(10xxxxxx gives 0x00, 110xxxxx 0xFF, 111xxxxx 0x80) with compares, masks and a select: nine NEON instructions. shufb
was 11% of GTA V's translated SPU samples (run 137b). Now (c ^ 0x80) >> 3 indexes a 16-byte table of the special values
for those bytes and is 16 or more for the others, which an extending table lookup (tbx) leaves as picked: five
instructions. Other hosts keep the portable code.

- Checked: the same result as the old code for 2 million random operands and for every control byte value (a scratch
  test), the differential fuzz test with 1,000 contexts per case.
- Measured (run 140, GTA V's walk, 60-90 s): the main SPU threads 6.95 to 6.91 s of CPU per 5 s, the audio SPU 1.57
  to 1.55. That is within the noise between runs, but never slower; kept for fewer instructions with the same results.

## D-219 · 2026-10-07 · SPU functions load registers where they are needed and store only what changed

Each lifted SPU function loaded every register it uses when it was entered and stored every register it writes on
every way out. Function entry loads were 9.4% of GTA V's translated SPU samples, calls 9.5% (run 137b).

- **Two analyses per function** (recomp/spu/src/lifter.cpp, RegFlow), mirroring how each instruction is lowered:
  forward, the "dirty" registers (written since the entry on some path, so ctx may not hold them; a call stores what
  the callee can touch, a stop or an indirect call stores everything); backward, the live registers, where every
  store of dirty registers counts as a read (the local must hold the right value whichever path led there).
- **Entry.** Called at its entry (ctx->pc is the entry), a function loads only the registers live there. Resumed
  anywhere else by the run loop it loads all it uses, as before.
- **Ways out.** Each stores only the dirty registers at that point: one exit block per distinct set. Around a direct
  call the caller stores the dirty registers the callee can touch (D-216 stored all it had written) and loads
  afterwards only the live ones the callee can write; after a stop or an indirect call only the live ones.
- **Indirect jumps** continue inside the function only at labels the analyzer found such jumps may reach
  (Function::dynamic: jump table targets, code addresses formed by constants, seeds that were not labels anyway).
  Anything else, a return above all, leaves: to the calling C function, which continues when the return address is
  its call's, or to the run loop. Before, every label was a possible target, so the dirty set of every return flowed
  to every label. Seeds that are labels anyway come from scripts/lift-spu.sh, which carries all of the previous lift's
  labels over as seeds. A side effect: a loop that goes round only through an indirect jump to its own function's
  label (improve.md, run 101) now passes the run loop's attention check, except at those labels.
- **Statically**, GTA V's 150 programs (4,056 functions): registers loaded at entry 192,707 to 86,743 (45%), stores
  per way out 46.4 to 42.9; a dispatch switch for indirect jumps in 97 functions. The C is 4% longer.
- **Checked:** a lifter unit test (tests/spu/test_lift_regs.cpp); the program-level fuzz program gained a callee that
  writes a register on one path only and one that writes before it reads, run against the interpreter; clang's
  uninitialised-use warnings (errors here) over all of GTA V's lifted code, which would catch a load the analysis
  missed on any path: none; the differential fuzz test; spu-check over all 150 of GTA V's programs (5,002 trials, no
  difference); the gate (PASS).
- **Measured** (run 141, GTA V's walk, 60-90 s, before and after in the same session): the main SPU threads 7.00 to
  6.56 s of CPU per 5 s (-6%), the audio SPU 1.57 to 1.39 (-11%), the process 11.9 to 11.2.

## D-220 · 2026-10-07 · The SPU module tracker knows each 16-byte line's run

The module tracker (D-079) watched every SPU GET into local store as runs of contiguous copies, listed in the 1 KB
blocks they touched; each GET tested the runs of its blocks and cut the ones it wrote over. In Assassin's Creed's crowd
(1.6 to 3 million GETs a second, 85% of them 256 bytes or less) that was about 240 ns a GET, 11-12% of the SPU threads'
busy time (runs 126-127). A free-slot list and run extents kept in the blocks had changed nothing (reverted then).

- **Line owners.** Each 16-byte line of local store holds the run that wrote it last (16,384 per SPU thread). A GET
  takes its lines from the runs that held them (each is identified again when it runs next: what was written may be its
  code), then extends the last run (contiguous in local store and in guest memory) or starts one. The run holding pc is
  its line's; the part of it still in local store is the stretch of lines around pc it still holds. So data copied into
  the middle of a module leaves both parts known, where D-204 kept only the part before the copy.
- **Runs live while they hold a line.** Each run counts its lines and its slot is freed at zero: a module loaded once
  stays known however many copies go elsewhere afterwards (it is looked up again every time execution comes back to it
  from the task's own code). A first draft kept only the newest 4,096 runs, which in the crowd is a few milliseconds of
  GETs: modules would have dropped to the interpreter. 4,096 slots; when all hold lines (a game copying thousands of
  tiny pieces) the next one round is given up, its lines cleared, as before.
- **Forgetting is one increment.** A line names its run by slot and epoch; a task switch (forget_module_runs) starts a
  new epoch, and lines of another epoch hold no run. Every million epochs the table is cleared once.
- A GET of fewer than 16 bytes takes its whole line, so a module whose code shares a 16-byte line with a variable the
  program DMAs into loses that line (the old tracker was exact to the byte). Not seen: the counts of modules lifted and
  instructions interpreted are unchanged in both games.

Measured (runs 142-149, before and after alternating in one session): Assassin's Creed's crowd, the SPU threads 13.16
to 11.59 and 14.56 to 12.79 s of CPU per 5 s (-12% both times), the process -8 to -10%; SPU code interpreted 184
instructions and 56,400 to 57,100 modules lifted either way. GTA V: within the noise between runs (its SPU code copies
far less), the same modules lifted, none interpreted; the gate passes.

Tests: tests/hle/test_spu_programs.cpp (data into a module's middle leaves its code part lifted; the module still known
after 10,000 copies elsewhere, more than the tracker has slots; D-204's and D-206's cases unchanged).

## D-222 · 2026-10-07 · A job chain remembers what each job's descriptor held when it took the job

GTA V's EDGE/GFX job chain stops now and then on a descriptor that holds something else (D-130, D-131, D-138, run 100;
on the Mac about one walk in ten: inventory/repro-edge, run2-3, a descriptor full of the game's own RSX state commands
and no SPU write over it). One explanation was ours: a job's descriptor is read when the job starts, up to three jobs
after the visit that took it, where libsre's pipeline (FETCH, INPUT, EXECUTE, OUTPUT) reads it about two jobs ahead; a
game reusing a descriptor once the chain has taken it would then hand us its new contents.

- **At the grab** the chain now keeps a hash of what the job uses (its header, input DMA list and cache list) and the
  header itself; **at the start** it hashes again. A difference is counted ("job descriptors changed between their
  grab and their start" at the end of a run), the first 20 are logged with both headers and the SPU writes over the
  descriptor since the grab, and a job chain stop's report (D-138) now begins with the descriptor as it was at the
  grab.
- **Measured:** GTA V's walk for 300 s (run 152): 0 changes. The theory is ruled out for normal play. A first version
  hashed all 0x280 bytes the chain reads per descriptor and found 28,518 changes in 300 s (run 150): all past +0x200,
  where GTA V's EDGE jobs put other jobs' output (the descriptors are 0x200 apart). Nothing a job uses.
- What is left: the next stop's report will say whether the descriptor was already broken when the job was taken (a
  stale command in the list, or the game's command buffer laid over a slot before the chain reached it) or changed
  after (a writer). The cost: two hashes of about 0x100 bytes per job.

## D-223 · 2026-10-07 · The module tracker scans lines eight at a time; a job chain hashes descriptors after its release

A profile of GTA V's walk (run 157, `sample` on the five main SPU threads) still found the module tracker's release
(D-220) at about 3% of their busy time: GTA V loads its modules in 16 KB GETs, 1,024 lines each, and release walked
them one at a time.

- **release** finds where a run's lines end eight at a time (two NEON compares and a horizontal minimum); other hosts
  keep the plain loop. Its samples 311 to 100 (runs 157, 171); GTA V's main SPU threads 6.67 and 6.45 to 6.40 and 6.40
  s of CPU per 5 s (runs 167-170, alternating), the process 11.39 and 11.06 to 11.01 and 10.96.
- **D-222's hashes** of the jobs a visit took are made after the visit releases the chain, not while other SPUs wait
  for its lock.
- **Tried, not kept** (runs 158-166): the same profile showed the SPU threads yielding about 12% of their busy time, a
  third of it waiting for the EDGE/GFX chain's lock. Sleeping on the chain's line (ps_res_wait_change) after 32 looks
  instead of yielding removed that, but the threads then piled up on the SPURS line in the workload selection (select1)
  and the SPU threads' CPU rose 5% under load; the idle Mac was unchanged. Reverted; the SPURS line is the item now
  (improve.md).

## D-224 · 2026-10-07 · A job chain stop reports its batch and the chain's last visits

D-222's grab snapshot showed GTA V's EDGE/GFX stops with the descriptor already other data when the chain took the job
(repro-edge2 run 1, runs 173, 178, 179): not changed after the grab, never a descriptor for this job. To see where the
command came from, each chain keeps its last 64 visits (by any SPU: pc before and after, the commands read, the jobs
taken; written without locks, read only by a report), and a stop's report lists them oldest first with every job of the
failing batch (its header at the grab and now). The report is printed once per stop (the error path and the fatal stop
both asked). The visits of the next stop (repro-edge2 run 26) found the cause, D-225.

## D-225 · 2026-10-07 · An SPU PUT writes its first eight bytes in one store

The visits before repro-edge2 run 26's stop: the chain waited on an END at 0x1074ca00, the game appended a JOB there and
a new END at 0x1074ca08, then rewrote that END: a visit read it as **0x00000000_00000012**, a light sync, passed it
(no jobs in flight) and took the next four commands, the previous lap's, whose descriptors the game had long reused
(garbage, floats, zeros; only the fourth still held a whole descriptor). Memory a moment later:
0x1074ca08 a JOB, 0x1074ca10 an END. The game had been turning the END into a jump-to-self (0x00000008_00000012),
written by an SPU job with an 8-byte PUT, and D-124 writes every PUT longer than a word with its first word last: the
low word (0x12) first, alone in memory until the high word (0x8) landed. On the Cell an aligned 8-byte DMA lands whole.
Under load the SPU thread can be preempted between the two stores, which is why the stop needed a busy machine (the
iPhone always is) and why it came about once in ten walks under load since D-124.

- **The fix:** a PUT longer than four bytes copies all but its first eight bytes, then stores those eight with one
  release store. D-124's purpose holds (the RSX parked on a block's first word sees the block whole once that word
  changes) and no command of eight bytes can be seen half written.
- D-125 saw the other half of the same tearing (a JTS turning into a JOB showing 0x00000008_<job EA>) and blamed the
  PPU; its wait on the JTS bit stays as a net.
- Test: tests/spu/test_interp_branch_mem.cpp, one thread PUTs a JTS and an END alternately into a doubleword, another
  reads it whole: without the fix it sees halves (3 of 3 runs), with it never.
- Measured: GTA V's walk under a load of six spinning threads, where it had stopped in 3 of 10 walks (repro-edge2 run 1,
  runs 178, repro-edge2 run 26): 0 stops in 11 walks of 150 s (repro-edge2 runs 41-51; run 40 was cut short, the Mac
  apparently asleep). The gate passes. An adversarial review (four lenses, two refuters per finding) found nothing that stood;
  the test now waits for its reader and checks every PUT landed.

## D-226 · 2026-10-07 · Preparing a game translates the SPU programs its executable carries

A game's SPU programs came only from images its runs had saved: on the phone, a game met for the first time ran all of
its SPU code interpreted until the next launch prepared it again (route B; docs/plan-game-modules.md, from a design
workflow: four readers, three designs, three judges). The executable's own SPU ELFs (SPURS tasks, SPU thread images) were
never looked for, though the system library has found its modules' since D-191.

- **The scan:** preparation reads the executable's PT_LOADs for SPU ELF headers (recomp::scan_spu_images) and saves each
  program as the runtime saves an image it meets: the executable segment holding the entry at its vaddr (what SPURS's
  task start and sys_spu_thread_group_start identify), the other executable segments as overlays. The saver is now
  shared with the system library (runtime/prepare/src/spu_static.cpp; the system library's output unchanged).
- **Tasks and the rest:** an image entered below 0x3000 cannot be a SPURS task (SPURS refuses such an entry): it is
  position independent code a program copies in, saved as a module and lifted relocatable, found at any local store
  address. Others are lifted where they sit.
- **Two inputs:** the SPU lift reads several folders; an image in more than one is the first folder's (the runs' copy,
  which knows how the game used it), with the seeds of all.
- **Prepared again once:** a game library records kGameInputsGeneration (1); an older one is prepared again. The system
  library is not asked (its inputs come from the firmware).
- **Measured:** GTA V's executable carries 8 SPU ELFs, Assassin's Creed's 6. Assassin's Creed prepared with no saved
  images (as the phone meets it): 6 programs from the executable, 4 tasks at 0x3000 under exactly the names its runs
  saved and 2 position independent ones at 0x80 (never met in our walks). A 150 s session on that library (run 207):
  the task it runs there found translated (never "no lifted program"); most of its SPU time is in modules that task
  copies in from game data (19 billion instructions interpreted at LS 0x2fba0), which only a run finds today: the next
  step.
- Tests: tests/game/test_prepare_spu.cpp (an executable's SPU ELFs saved under the runtime's names, a task where it
  sits, position independent ones relocatable, two folders lifted with the seeds of both); test_game_library.cpp (the
  inputs generation).

## D-227 · 2026-10-07 · A build deletes the objects nothing links any more

Each object is named by everything that makes it (source, settings, include folders), so a re-preparation keeps what is
unchanged (D-209) and compiles the rest, but nothing ever deleted the objects of sources that changed or went: every
time a game met new SPU programs, or the translator changed, the old objects stayed. Assassin's Creed's prepared folder
on the Mac held 2,957 objects (637 MB) for a build of 418. On the phone that is storage gone with every update.

- After a successful link, codegen::build_library deletes the .o files of its object folder that this build neither
  compiled nor kept; other files are left alone, and nothing is deleted when the build fails.
- Measured: Assassin's Creed prepared again in place (with D-226's executable programs): 2,545 objects deleted (566 MB),
  the folder 637 to 89 MB, in 12 s (411 files kept, 6 compiled).
- Test: tests/game/test_game_library.cpp (a changed source's old object deleted, the unchanged one kept, a file that is
  not an object left).

"No interpreting" has to be measured per game, and the PPU report (D-207) listed only addresses. pspocket-boot's
end-of-run report now names whose code each interpreted site is (the executable, a firmware module in the PRX region,
a module the game loaded, or other code: HLE stubs, code made in memory) and sums the instructions per owner. The app,
which never read the counters, logs every 5 s how many PPU and SPU instructions the interpreters ran since the last
line, when there were any. Assassin's Creed, 90 s (run 208): 196,608 PPU instructions, all the executable's (its fiber
resumes, D-161), and the SPU's 184 at the one module entry D-208 left.

Tried: reading the words a packet still has in one inner loop (one acquire per word still, get published once at the
